questions.title: Ciphertext
questions.q: Cipher text is the scrambled and unreadable output of encryption.
questions.answer: TRUE. Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. Decryption recovers plaintext using the appropriate key. Hashing instead produces a digest for comparison and has no decryption operation.
questions.teach: Plaintext is the readable message. Ciphertext is its encrypted representation. A digest is a different kind of output.
questions.example: A payroll file is encrypted before transfer. Someone who intercepts the file sees ciphertext and needs the appropriate decryption key to read it.
questions.correct: True
distractors: False
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Ciphertext in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: False

setting.object: A private report stored as an encrypted file.
setting.location: A laptop’s storage drive and the application opening the file.
setting.purpose: Let authorized people recover the report while protecting it from unauthorized reading.
setting.action: Encryption transforms the contents into ciphertext; the appropriate decryption procedure and key recover plaintext.
setting.example: A payroll file is encrypted before transfer. Someone who intercepts the file sees ciphertext and needs the appropriate decryption key to read it.

questions.title: Targets beyond payment data
questions.q: Attackers target personal information beyond credit-card numbers and bank-account numbers to make money. True or false?
questions.answer: CC means credit card. The # symbol means number here: CC# means credit-card number, and bank account# means bank-account number. The statement says criminals also profit from other personal information, such as passwords, identity details, and medical records. TRUE. Personal information, credentials, health records, private communications, and intellectual property can support fraud, extortion, resale, and espionage. The textbook’s social-engineering example shows why account-recovery information can be valuable even without a full card number.
questions.teach: CC means credit card. The # symbol means number here: CC# means credit-card number, and bank account# means bank-account number. The statement says criminals also profit from other personal information, such as passwords, identity details, and medical records.
questions.example: An attacker steals a student’s login and recovery information, then uses the account to impersonate the student or access additional services.
questions.correct: True
distractors: False
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Targets beyond payment data in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: False

setting.object: A stolen student login, address, and medical information.
setting.location: Account records and private files accessed through a compromised account.
setting.purpose: Understand why personal information is valuable even without payment-card details.
setting.action: An attacker may use stolen information for impersonation, fraud, resale, or extortion.
setting.example: An attacker steals a student’s login and recovery information, then uses the account to impersonate the student or access additional services.

questions.title: SET and stealth
questions.q: SET-based attack has become more popular these days due to its stealthy penetration.
questions.answer: TRUE. SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) means Social-Engineer Toolkit. Your SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) lab shows that a convincing fake login page can capture credentials through user interaction, and a redirect can conceal the deception. The key concept is social engineering: deception persuades the user to disclose information, reducing the attacker’s dependence on exploiting a software vulnerability.
questions.teach: A user trusts a deceptive page and submits credentials. A familiar appearance and a redirect to the real site can make the credential theft less noticeable.
questions.example: A fully patched employee enters a password on a cloned login page. The password is disclosed without exploiting a software flaw. Login monitoring and phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) reduce the resulting risk.
questions.correct: True
distractors: False because SET cannot collect credentials
True because SET always bypasses every control
False because SET is an encryption algorithm
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) and stealth in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: False because SET cannot collect credentials

setting.object: A staff member enters a test password into a cloned login page.
setting.location: The employee’s browser and a credential-collection page in the authorized lab.
setting.purpose: Understand how a convincing page can obtain credentials through user interaction.
setting.action: The form submits the entered information to the collecting system. This alone does not prove malicious code ran on the employee’s computer.
setting.example: A fully patched employee enters a password on a cloned login page. The password is disclosed without exploiting a software flaw. Login monitoring and phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) reduce the resulting risk.

questions.title: Reverse shell and firewall limits
questions.q: The reverse shell attack is capable of defeating packet filtering firewall but not proxy firewall.
questions.answer: FALSE as written. A reverse shell starts an outbound connection from a compromised internal host to an attacker. It can pass packet filters that allow that outbound traffic. A proxy can require authentication, restrict destinations and protocols, and inspect traffic, but its effectiveness depends on configuration and visibility. A properly configured proxy can block a raw shell connection by enforcing application protocols. A shell tunneled through an allowed application protocol still requires inspection and policy enforcement; the word proxy alone does not guarantee prevention.
questions.teach: Direction and policy explain the result. Outbound does not mean automatically allowed, and proxy does not mean automatically secure.
questions.example: A workstation makes an unusual outbound connection after a malicious process starts. Correlate process and network logs, isolate the host, and restrict unnecessary egress rather than relying solely on inbound rules.
questions.correct: False: firewall effectiveness depends on its rules and inspection
distractors: Always true for every proxy
False because reverse shells only start inbound connections
True because a proxy encrypts every endpoint process
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Reverse shell and firewall limits in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Always true for every proxy

setting.object: A compromised workstation starts a command connection to an outside controller.
setting.location: A program on the workstation and its outbound network connection.
setting.purpose: Understand remote command access and why outbound traffic needs appropriate controls.
setting.action: A reverse shell starts its connection from the affected computer. Filtering depends on rules, protocol handling, and visibility.
setting.example: A workstation makes an unusual outbound connection after a malicious process starts. Correlate process and network logs, isolate the host, and restrict unnecessary egress rather than relying solely on inbound rules.

questions.title: TCP/IP is a suite
questions.q: TCP/IP represent a suite of protocols including DNS, SNMP, SMPT, POP, and FTP etc.
questions.answer: TRUE with a spelling correction: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), not SMPT. TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) names a protocol suite spanning layers. DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) supports device management, SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail, POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves mail, and FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transfers files. They are not all transport-layer protocols.
questions.teach: The suite is the whole family. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) are central members with different jobs.
questions.example: A mail application resolves a server name with DNS (Domain Name System), connects using transport protocols, and uses SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) to send mail. Several suite members cooperate.
questions.correct: True
distractors: False
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) is a suite in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: False

setting.object: A computer looks up a mail server, sends a message, and retrieves mail.
setting.location: The client, DNS (Domain Name System) service, mail servers, and network connections.
setting.purpose: Distinguish the communication jobs performed by different protocols.
setting.action: DNS (Domain Name System) looks up names; SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail; POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves mail. TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) is a family of cooperating protocols.
setting.example: A mail application resolves a server name with DNS (Domain Name System), connects using transport protocols, and uses SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) to send mail. Several suite members cooperate.

questions.title: Security job roles
questions.q: Ian analyzes and designs security solutions and identifies users’ needs. Which position is this?
questions.answer: A. Security administrator. Ciampa Chapter 1, printed page 6 (PDF page 34), assigns these duties to the security administrator. A technician configures and troubleshoots tools; a manager supervises personnel; the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) directs security at the executive level. This resolves the second guide’s textbook-needed placeholder.
questions.teach: Match the duties to this textbook’s definition. Job titles at actual companies can vary.
questions.example: An employee evaluates staff security needs and designs a suitable access-control solution while managing daily security technology. That matches the administrator role in the book.
questions.correct: Security administrator
distractors: Security technician
Security officer
Security manager
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Security job roles in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Security technician

setting.object: An organization hires staff to design security, configure tools, and supervise the team.
setting.location: The organization’s security department and its supported systems.
setting.purpose: Match a job’s actual duties to the textbook’s role definitions.
setting.action: The administrator designs solutions for users, the technician configures and troubleshoots tools, and the manager supervises personnel.
setting.example: An employee evaluates staff security needs and designs a suitable access-control solution while managing daily security technology. That matches the administrator role in the book.

questions.title: Race condition
questions.q: What is a race condition?
questions.answer: D. Concurrent execution accesses shared state without adequate synchronization, so the result depends on timing or ordering and can become unintended. A race condition is a concurrency flaw, not a synonym for DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service), slow processing, or a race to patch before attackers act.
questions.teach: Two operations interfere because each assumes it can use the same state safely. Locking, atomic operations, or safe transaction design can prevent this.
questions.example: Two checkout requests both see one remaining item before either updates stock. Both complete, selling the same item twice.
questions.correct: Concurrent execution accesses a shared resource and causes unintended consequences
distractors: A race to patch a newly discovered vulnerability
A software update released before discovery
An attack finishing before antivirus scanning
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Race condition in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A race to patch a newly discovered vulnerability

setting.object: Two checkout requests both try to buy the last item in stock.
setting.location: Concurrent operations in the store’s application and shared stock record.
setting.purpose: Prevent conflicting operations from producing an unintended result.
setting.action: If both requests read the old stock value before either updates it, timing can cause an incorrect result. Safe synchronization or transactions address the race.
setting.example: Two checkout requests both see one remaining item before either updates stock. Both complete, selling the same item twice.

questions.title: Vishing
questions.q: Which statement is correct about vishing?
questions.answer: C. VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) makes caller-ID spoofing easier. Vishing is voice phishing: an attacker uses a call or voice message to trick someone into revealing information or performing an action. Calls can be automated, targeted, or broadly distributed; it does not always require a live person.
questions.teach: Voice is the identifying feature. Caller ID is a claim, not proof of identity.
questions.example: A caller claims to be the help desk and asks for a login code. Hang up and verify through an independently known help-desk number.
questions.correct: VoIP makes caller-ID spoofing easier
distractors: It is only tailored to organizations
It only targets large organizations
It always uses a real person to call
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Vishing in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: It is only tailored to organizations

setting.object: A caller pretends to be campus IT (Information Technology) and asks for a login code.
setting.location: A phone call or voice message received by an employee.
setting.purpose: Recognize voice-based deception and verify identity through a trusted channel.
setting.action: Vishing uses voice to manipulate the recipient. A displayed caller number can be spoofed and is not proof of identity.
setting.example: A caller claims to be the help desk and asks for a login code. Hang up and verify through an independently known help-desk number.

questions.title: Email sender investigation
questions.q: To investigate a phishing email, where would you go for sender information?
questions.answer: D. Email header. Full headers provide routing and sender-related fields such as Received, Return-Path, and authentication results. Compare these with the claimed sender and timestamps. A display name, body, attachment, or embedded URL (Uniform Resource Locator) alone does not establish who sent the message. Some header fields can also be forged; establish trusted receiving-system boundaries.
questions.teach: Headers provide evidence for investigation. Reading the visible sender label alone is not enough.
questions.example: An email claims to come from campus IT (Information Technology) but uses a lookalike domain and urgent password language. Preserve the message and inspect headers through the approved reporting process.
questions.correct: Email header
distractors: Attachment
Embedded URL
Email body
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Email sender investigation in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Attachment

setting.object: An email claims the recipient must urgently reset a university password.
setting.location: The received message, full headers, links, and mail-system records.
setting.purpose: Investigate the claimed sender and request without trusting the display name.
setting.action: Compare routing and authentication evidence, sender domains, timing, and the request with a trusted reporting or verification process.
setting.example: An email claims to come from campus IT (Information Technology) but uses a lookalike domain and urgent password language. Preserve the message and inspect headers through the approved reporting process.

questions.title: Static analysis terminology
questions.q: Which of the following is a static analysis tool: Firebug, McAfee Advisor, JSUnpack, Norton SafeWeb, or OpenSSL?
questions.answer: C. JSUnpack. It unpacks and analyzes suspicious JavaScript to expose concealed code and URLs. Remember the underlying distinction: static analysis inspects code without running it; dynamic analysis observes execution. JSUnpack also uses emulation, so its capabilities extend beyond static inspection. Firebug is a browser debugger, SiteAdvisor and Safe Web are reputation services, and OpenSSL is a cryptographic toolkit. Static analysis examines code without executing it; dynamic analysis observes execution.
questions.teach: Associate JSUnpack with unpacking suspicious JavaScript. Static versus dynamic describes whether code executes; manual versus automated describes who or what performs the analysis.
questions.example: Reading script text and decoding an embedded string without running the script is static work. Observing redirects while script executes in an isolated environment is dynamic work.
questions.correct: JSUnpack
distractors: McAfee Advisor is a source-code compiler
Norton SafeWeb is an offline disassembler
OpenSSL is a browser reputation database
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Static analysis terminology in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: McAfee Advisor is a source-code compiler

setting.object: An analyst examines a suspicious web page and its scripts.
setting.location: Page source, an isolated test browser, and website-analysis services.
setting.purpose: Determine what the page does and interpret the evidence behind a safety rating.
setting.action: Static analysis inspects without executing; dynamic analysis observes execution. Manual and automated describe who performs the work; reputation summarizes observations.
setting.example: Reading script text and decoding an embedded string without running the script is static work. Observing redirects while script executes in an isolated environment is dynamic work.

questions.title: TCP reliability
questions.q: Which protocol is responsible for data packet quality and basic security features in transmission?
questions.answer: A. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). Transmission Control Protocol provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery using acknowledgments, retransmissions, sequencing, and a checksum. IP (Internet Protocol) supplies addressing and routing. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)’s reliability and checksum are not confidentiality or cryptographic authentication. HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) security at a different level.
questions.teach: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) handles reliable delivery. It does not itself encrypt your message or prove the other party’s identity.
questions.example: A file download needs all bytes in order. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) can retransmit missing data; TLS (Transport Layer Security) is needed separately to protect confidentiality and authenticate the server.
questions.correct: TCP
distractors: IP
UDP
HTTP
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reliability in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: IP

setting.object: A laptop sends file data to a server across a network.
setting.location: The application, transport service, IP (Internet Protocol) network, and local links.
setting.purpose: Understand which layer handles reliable delivery, separate messages, and forwarding.
setting.action: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides separate datagrams without those guarantees; IP (Internet Protocol) forwards packets toward destinations.
setting.example: A file download needs all bytes in order. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) can retransmit missing data; TLS (Transport Layer Security) is needed separately to protect confidentiality and authenticate the server.

questions.title: False positive
questions.q: An IDS raises an alarm on normal, nonmalicious traffic. What error is this?
questions.answer: False positive, also called a Type I error in your notes. A false negative (Type II) occurs when malicious traffic is treated as benign. False positives consume analyst time and can interrupt legitimate work if prevention blocks the traffic; false negatives leave attacks undetected.
questions.teach: Positive means the system says threat. False means that conclusion is wrong.
questions.example: A legitimate backup triggers a malware alert: false positive. A real malicious download produces no alert: false negative.
questions.correct: False positive
distractors: False negative
True positive
True negative
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain False positive in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: False negative

setting.object: A monitoring system warns about a network transfer that may be an attack or a legitimate backup.
setting.location: The security alert and the network or host activity that triggered it.
setting.purpose: Decide whether the alert represents a real problem and choose an appropriate response.
setting.action: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) alerts; IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can intervene. Investigated evidence helps tune rules without hiding real attacks or unnecessarily blocking normal work.
setting.example: A legitimate backup triggers a malware alert: false positive. A real malicious download produces no alert: false negative.

questions.title: Dormant program and C2
questions.q: A program or part of a program lies dormant until triggered by the C2 server. What is it?
questions.answer: Bot. A malicious bot is a program on a compromised device that receives instructions from a command-and-control (C2 (Command and Control)) server. It can wait for a command before carrying out an action. A botnet is a collection of these controlled devices. Distinguish a logic bomb: code activated by a specified condition, such as a date or file deletion. A backdoor provides concealed access.
questions.teach: C2 (Command and Control) means command and control. In this question, the remote server issuing instructions identifies the program as a bot; the collection of controlled devices is a botnet.
questions.example: A timed destructive routine is a logic bomb. An infected workstation waiting for remote instructions is a bot. Both can be dormant, but they are classified by different behavior.
questions.correct: Bot
distractors: Checksum
Ciphertext
Firewall
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Dormant program and C2 (Command and Control) in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Checksum

setting.object: A malicious program on an infected computer waits for remote instructions.
setting.location: The infected device and a command-and-control server.
setting.purpose: Recognize the program’s remote-control role.
setting.action: A bot receives C2 (Command and Control) commands. A botnet is a collection of controlled devices; a logic bomb is classified by activation on a specified condition.
setting.example: A timed destructive routine is a logic bomb. An infected workstation waiting for remote instructions is a bot. Both can be dormant, but they are classified by different behavior.

questions.title: Hard fork
questions.q: What splits one blockchain instance into two through an incompatible protocol change?
questions.answer: Hard fork is the guide’s intended term. It changes consensus rules incompatibly, so nodes following different rules can maintain different chains. A persistent split depends on participants continuing both histories; a hard fork need not always leave two lasting communities. A soft fork tightens accepted rules compatibly for older nodes.
questions.teach: A protocol disagreement is different from two miners briefly finding competing blocks.
questions.example: One group adopts a rule that older nodes reject while another group continues the old rules. Their accepted transaction histories can diverge.
questions.correct: Hard fork
distractors: Checksum
Digital signature
Symmetric key
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Hard fork in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Checksum

setting.object: Two groups follow different rules for accepting blockchain records, or two payments try to spend the same funds.
setting.location: The transaction ledger maintained by participating computers.
setting.purpose: Understand agreement about which valid transaction history is accepted.
setting.action: Validation and consensus resolve competing histories. Incompatible rule changes can produce a hard fork when participants continue separate histories.
setting.example: One group adopts a rule that older nodes reject while another group continues the old rules. Their accepted transaction histories can diverge.

questions.title: Checksum
questions.q: What tool checks integrity of packet content?
questions.answer: Checksum. The receiver recomputes an error-detection value and compares it with the transmitted value to detect accidental corruption. An ordinary Internet checksum is not SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) and does not defend against an attacker who can alter data and recompute the checksum. Cryptographic integrity requires a suitable authenticated mechanism such as a MAC or signature.
questions.teach: An error check catches transmission damage. Authenticating malicious changes requires a stronger, trusted construction.
questions.example: A bit flips while a segment is transmitted and the checksum comparison fails. The receiver can discard it; reliable transport may retransmit.
questions.correct: Checksum
distractors: Ciphertext
Public key
Nonce
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Checksum in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Ciphertext

setting.object: A network segment may have been corrupted during transmission.
setting.location: The transmitted data and the receiver’s error-checking calculation.
setting.purpose: Detect accidental changes to the received contents.
setting.action: The receiver recalculates a checksum and compares it with the transmitted value. An ordinary checksum does not authenticate the sender against deliberate changes.
setting.example: A bit flips while a segment is transmitted and the checksum comparison fails. The receiver can discard it; reliable transport may retransmit.

questions.title: Why patching becomes easier
questions.q: How do bandwidth, cloud computing, big data/analytics, and virtualization alleviate security-update pressure?
questions.answer: More bandwidth speeds patch distribution, although deployments still need scheduling. Cloud-based and centralized management can coordinate updates across fleets, while customers retain responsibilities for their own systems and configurations. Analytics helps inventory systems, prioritize exposure, and detect failed updates. Virtualization supports representative test environments, snapshots, and rollback. Together these reduce transfer, coordination, decision, and testing costs. They do not remove compatibility testing, outages, or zero-day risk.
questions.teach: Organize your discussion by the bottleneck each technology reduces. State one benefit and one limitation for each.
questions.example: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available.
questions.correct: Distribution, coordination, prioritization, and safe testing become easier
distractors: All updates can be installed without testing
Snapshots eliminate the need for backups
Cloud providers automatically patch every customer application
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Why patching becomes easier in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: All updates can be installed without testing

setting.object: An IT (Information Technology) team must install security updates on many company computers without breaking work.
setting.location: Update distribution, test devices, deployment records, and production systems.
setting.purpose: Repair weaknesses efficiently while verifying that needed services still work.
setting.action: Bandwidth helps distribute updates; centralized services coordinate; analytics prioritizes; virtual machines support testing. Stage changes and verify the results.
setting.example: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available.

questions.title: Viruses and other malware
questions.q: What are the major types of computer viruses, and how do virus, worm, scareware, adware, spyware, and backdoor differ?
questions.answer: A virus attaches to a host file or document and replicates when the host runs; a worm is a standalone program that can propagate across networks. Scareware uses fraudulent alarms to pressure payment or installation. Adware displays unwanted advertising; spyware secretly collects information; a backdoor bypasses normal access controls. In this textbook’s Chapter 2, viruses include program/file viruses and macro viruses, with appender infection and armored concealment techniques: Swiss cheese, split infection, oligomorphic, polymorphic, and metamorphic mutation. Boot-sector viruses are another common category, but the supplied edition emphasizes the preceding list. The guide labels this Ch. 1; the relevant detail is actually Ch. 2, pp. 55–65.
questions.teach: Compare how malware spreads, hides, and acts. These categories can overlap: a backdoor may install spyware that includes a keylogger.
questions.example: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense.
questions.correct: Virus needs a host; worm propagates independently; other names describe behavior
distractors: All malware is a virus
Scareware is legitimate antivirus
Backdoors are the same as checksums
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Viruses and other malware in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: All malware is a virus

setting.object: An employee opens an infected program or document, or a malicious program spreads between computers.
setting.location: Program files, documents, running software, and networked devices.
setting.purpose: Identify how malicious software propagates and what harmful behavior it performs.
setting.action: A virus attaches to a host; a worm propagates independently. Spyware observes, adware displays ads, scareware deceives with warnings, and a backdoor provides concealed access.
setting.example: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense.

questions.title: Confidentiality authentication obfuscation
questions.q: How do confidentiality, authentication, and obfuscation correlate in cryptographic applications?
questions.answer: Confidentiality limits who can read data, usually through encryption. Authentication establishes a claimed identity or data origin through a suitable cryptographic protocol; a digital signature can bind a message to a signing key. Obfuscation makes information or implementation details harder to understand, and the textbook includes it among cryptographic protections. These goals complement one another but do not substitute for one another. Encryption to a recipient’s public key does not by itself identify the sender; an ordinary hash does not authenticate an origin; signing does not encrypt the message. For secrecy plus sender authentication, use a properly designed encrypted and authenticated scheme.
questions.teach: Ask three separate questions: who can read, who created or approved it, and what details are being obscured?
questions.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.
questions.correct: Encryption protects reading; authentication proves origin; obfuscation obscures details
distractors: A hash alone proves the sender
A signature automatically hides the message
Obfuscation always replaces encryption
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
rubric: Explain why obfuscation alone is insufficient
questions.goal: Explain Confidentiality authentication obfuscation in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A hash alone proves the sender

setting.object: A business sends a private document and needs to detect changes or verify its approval.
setting.location: The document, any encrypted representation, its computed digest, and any digital signature.
setting.purpose: Choose the operation that fits confidentiality, content comparison, or origin verification.
setting.action: Encryption hides readable content; a trusted hash comparison checks content; a signature supports verification under a trusted signing key. These operations are not interchangeable.
setting.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.

questions.title: Collision resistance
questions.q: Hash algorithms are naturally resistant to hash collisions. Why?
questions.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.
questions.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.
questions.example: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison.
questions.correct: Large well-distributed outputs make finding collisions computationally difficult
distractors: Collisions are mathematically impossible
Hashing encrypts every input uniquely
All hash algorithms have equal collision resistance
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Collision resistance in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Collisions are mathematically impossible

setting.object: A downloaded file is compared with a publisher’s trusted reference digest.

questions.title: Blockchain mechanics and tradeoffs
questions.q: How does blockchain work? What are its pros and cons?
questions.answer: Transactions are grouped into blocks. A block header commits to transaction data through a Merkle root and includes the previous block’s hash. Altering data changes its hash and breaks later commitments. Nodes validate transactions and consensus determines the accepted history. In Bitcoin, proof of work requires miners to search nonces for a header hash meeting a target; the accepted valid chain has the greatest cumulative work. More confirmations make rewriting history harder under the network’s security assumptions. Benefits include shared auditability and tamper evidence. Costs include proof-of-work energy use, throughput/latency limits, public-data privacy issues, key loss, and difficult correction of erroneous entries. Blockchain is not an absolute guarantee of truth or immutability, and not all blockchains use proof of work.
questions.teach: Hashes connect history; signatures authorize spending; consensus resolves competing histories. None does all three jobs alone.
questions.example: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part.
questions.correct: Hash links plus validation and consensus create a shared tamper-evident history
distractors: Encryption alone makes every transaction private
A nonce is the owner’s password
Every blockchain must use Bitcoin mining

questions.title: Bitcoin and ownership transfer
questions.q: What is a bitcoin?
questions.answer: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer digital currency whose transaction history is recorded on a blockchain. A spender authorizes use of earlier unspent transaction outputs by satisfying their spending conditions, typically with a digital signature created using the spender’s private key. A new output specifies conditions for the receiver. Nodes verify authorization and check for double spending; mining orders valid transactions through proof of work. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) contributes to hashing and proof of work, not encryption of a coin. An address is commonly derived from a key or script and is not always the raw public key. Public ledger transparency provides pseudonymity, not guaranteed anonymity. Miners receive a block subsidy and transaction fees as incentives.
questions.teach: Ownership means the ability to authorize spending under the output’s rules. You transfer spending rights through a transaction; you do not email a secret coin file.
questions.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.
questions.correct: A peer-to-peer currency with signature-authorized spending and blockchain consensus
distractors: A coin encrypted with SHA-256 and emailed
A central-bank database with no signatures
An anonymous password shared by all miners

questions.title: CIA and risk
questions.q: Which protection matches confidentiality, integrity, and availability respectively?
questions.answer: Confidentiality restricts disclosure, integrity protects against unauthorized alteration, and availability provides access when needed. An asset has value; a vulnerability is a weakness; a threat can cause harm; risk concerns likelihood and impact. Risk responses include accept, avoid, mitigate, and transfer. Controls can be technical, administrative, or physical.
questions.teach: Confidentiality means only permitted people can see the data. Integrity means the data is not changed without permission. Availability means authorized users can get the data or service when needed.
questions.example: A hospital considers ransomware risk to patient records. Backups improve recovery, access controls restrict disclosure, and monitoring detects changes.
questions.correct: Keep information private; prevent unauthorized changes; keep services usable by authorized people.
distractors: CPU, Internet, and antivirus
Only encryption strength
The same property under three names

questions.title: Threat actors and priorities
questions.q: How do motivations and access distinguish threat actors?
questions.answer: Organized crime often seeks profit; hacktivists pursue ideological goals; nation-state actors may seek espionage or disruption; insiders already have trusted access; script kiddies rely on existing tools; vulnerability brokers sell knowledge. Advanced persistent threats involve sustained, targeted activity. Zero-day describes an unknown or unpatched vulnerability context, not a person. Your notes emphasize social engineering and insiders as pressing concerns; actual priority depends on organizational exposure.

questions.title: Five defense principles
questions.q: Which example correctly applies the principles of layering, limiting, diversity, obscurity, and simplicity?
questions.answer: Layering adds multiple safeguards. Limiting gives only necessary access. Diversity reduces shared failure modes across products or controls. Obscurity hides unnecessary details but cannot be the sole defense. Simplicity makes controls easier to understand and manage. Frameworks and reference architectures organize a security program; some are regulatory, industry-specific, national, or international.
questions.teach: Layering means several protective layers. Limiting means giving only necessary access. Diversity reduces reliance on one kind of protection. Obscurity hides unnecessary information but cannot replace real security. Simplicity keeps controls understandable and manageable.
questions.example: Email filtering, a standard-user account, endpoint monitoring, and recovery procedures protect different points in a phishing incident.
questions.correct: Use multiple safeguards, grant only needed access, vary protection methods, hide unnecessary details, and keep rules understandable.
distractors: Publish all secrets to simplify access
Use only one secret product
Give all users administrator rights

questions.title: Defense in depth and architecture
questions.q: How should a business use choke points, visibility, availability, and scalability when designing defenses?
questions.answer: Use safeguards at both perimeter and endpoint. A choke point is a controlled entry or exit where traffic can be inspected; internal segmentation also matters. Visibility requires useful telemetry at these boundaries and on hosts. Redundancy reduces single points of failure, while scalability supports changing workload. Balance security with business availability, budget, and capacity. The castle analogy illustrates defense in depth: a gate, walls, guards, and internal locks protect different boundaries. In a business, filtering, MFA (Multi Factor Authentication), least privilege, application allowlisting, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), monitoring, and recovery provide complementary layers. If a phishing message passes the filter, other layers can still restrict execution, account access, lateral movement, and damage.
questions.teach: A choke point is a controlled place where traffic passes. Visibility means collecting evidence of activity. Availability means keeping services working. Scalability means handling growth. For example, a store checks traffic entering its network, keeps payment computers separate from other systems, records activity on staff devices, and provides a backup network device so one failure does not stop sales.
questions.example: A store checks traffic entering its network, separates payment computers from other computers, collects activity records from staff devices, and uses a backup device so one failure does not stop sales.
questions.correct: Inspect traffic at controlled entry points, collect useful records, provide backup paths, and plan for growing traffic.
distractors: A perimeter firewall eliminates all endpoint risk
Visibility means capturing only public web pages
Redundancy makes filtering rules unnecessary

questions.title: IDS versus IPS
questions.q: What is the difference between an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)?
questions.answer: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) detects suspicious activity and alerts. An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can actively block or disrupt traffic or activity. Either can use signatures, heuristics, behavior, or other techniques; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) does not require AI. Host IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) observes local activity; network controls observe traffic. Tune false positives and false negatives in light of business impact.
questions.teach: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) stands for Intrusion Detection System. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) stands for Intrusion Prevention System. Detection raises an alert. Prevention can take action to stop activity. Both need careful rules so normal work is not mistaken for an attack.
questions.example: An alert-only sensor reports suspicious traffic. An inline prevention rule blocks the same traffic, potentially interrupting legitimate service if the rule is wrong.
questions.correct: An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts; an IPS can also block or interrupt suspicious activity.
distractors: IDS always blocks packets
IPS always requires AI
An antivirus database makes false negatives impossible

questions.title: PCAP flow proxy and allowlisting
questions.q: Which description correctly distinguishes packet capture, flow records, a proxy, and application allowlisting?
questions.answer: Full PCAP (Packet Capture) records packet bytes within capture limits, useful for detailed reconstruction; encrypted payloads remain encrypted without suitable keys. Flow records summarize conversations such as endpoints, times, ports, and byte counts. A proxy mediates application requests and can enforce policy and log activity. Application allowlisting permits approved software and restricts other execution. These controls complement rather than replace one another.
questions.teach: Packet capture records observed packet contents within recording limits. Flow records summarize who communicated, when, and how much. A proxy receives and forwards application requests while applying rules. Application allowlisting prevents unapproved programs from running. These are four different jobs.
questions.example: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events.
questions.correct: Packet capture stores packet bytes; flow records summarize connections; a proxy handles requests; allowlisting controls which programs run.
distractors: Flow records always include every file
A proxy is the same as PCAP
Allowlisting permits all unknown programs

questions.title: DDoS SYN flood and Slowloris
questions.q: How do SYN flooding and Slowloris affect availability?
questions.answer: Denial of service exhausts resources or disrupts access; distributed DoS (Denial of Service) uses multiple sources. A SYN flood abuses half-open TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection state. Slowloris holds many HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) connections with incomplete, slow requests and may work from few sources. Mitigations include upstream filtering, rate and connection limits, appropriate timeouts, SYN protections, and capacity planning. DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) can distract responders but is not always a distraction or a race condition.
questions.teach: Bandwidth floods and application connection exhaustion stress different resources. Match mitigation to the bottleneck.
questions.example: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern.
questions.correct: They consume connection resources and deny legitimate access
distractors: All DoS attacks require a giant botnet
Slowloris encrypts a database
A SYN flood is simply a race condition

questions.title: SQL injection versus XSS
questions.q: What changes when malicious input reaches a SQL query versus a browser?
questions.answer: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection makes untrusted input influence database query structure. Parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL (Structured Query Language) commands; least-privilege database accounts limit harm. XSS (Cross Site Scripting) causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a user’s browser in a trusted site’s context. Use context-aware output encoding, safe APIs, and appropriate sanitization for allowed HTML (Hypertext Markup Language). Input validation supports both but is insufficient alone. WebGoat is a deliberately vulnerable teaching application. Neither attack is limited to one operating system. A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes beyond a buffer’s allocated boundary. It can corrupt adjacent memory, crash the program, or enable code execution. Prevent it through bounds checking, memory-safe programming, and patching; DEP/NX, ASLR, and stack protections add mitigation. SQL (Structured Query Language) injection instead changes a database command through unsafe input; XSS (Cross Site Scripting) executes injected content in a victim browser. These are different interpreters and require different defenses.
questions.teach: Ask where the injected content is interpreted: database query engine or victim browser. XSS (Cross Site Scripting) is not automatically full server control.
questions.example: A search value must remain a SQL (Structured Query Language) parameter. A comment displayed on a page must remain text or sanitized allowed HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) rather than executable script.
questions.correct: SQLi changes query interpretation; XSS executes script in the browser
distractors: Both are prevented by antivirus alone
XSS always takes full control of the application server
Prepared statements alone prevent every XSS flaw

questions.title: Social-engineering families
questions.q: How do phishing, spear phishing, smishing, vishing, and a 419 scam differ?
questions.answer: Phishing uses deceptive communication to elicit information or action. Spear phishing targets particular recipients using tailored context. Smishing uses SMS; vishing uses voice. A 419 or advance-fee scam promises a benefit to obtain money or sensitive data upfront. Scareware creates false security urgency. Verify requests through independent trusted channels and report suspicious messages.
questions.teach: Channel, targeting, and pretext distinguish these related attacks.
questions.example: An urgent campus-password message aimed at named students is targeted phishing. A phone request for login codes is vishing.

questions.title: Metasploit and SET business case
questions.q: What do the Metasploit and SET labs demonstrate for a business?
questions.answer: Metasploit organizes authorized security testing through exploit, payload, auxiliary, and post-exploitation capabilities. SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) is a separate TrustedSec social-engineering toolkit that can integrate with Metasploit; it is not simply a Metasploit module. The credential-harvesting lab demonstrates how user trust can disclose credentials without a software exploit. Prevent with training, filtering, phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication), and login monitoring. If credentials are disclosed, report, reset affected secrets from a trusted device, revoke sessions, and investigate related access. MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) combines distinct factor categories: something you know, have, or are. A password plus another password is not MFA (Multi Factor Authentication). MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) is a major defense against stolen passwords; phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO (Fast IDentity Online)/WebAuthn resist deceptive-site authentication. Account monitoring, session revocation, least privilege, and endpoint security remain necessary alongside MFA (Multi Factor Authentication).
questions.teach: Explain the weakness, business consequence, evidence, and defense. Exact tool-menu commands are not the stated exam priority.
questions.example: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions.
questions.correct: Structured testing and social-engineering simulation reveal technical and human weaknesses
distractors: SET is a hash algorithm
Patching alone prevents every fake-login attack
A captured password always means code executed on the host

questions.title: Keylogger and encryption boundaries
questions.q: Why can a keylogger steal information even when a website uses HTTPS?
questions.answer: A keylogger records input on the endpoint, often before TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts it for transport. Software variants may intercept input APIs, run with elevated privileges, or observe forms; hardware variants can sit between keyboard and computer. Not every keylogger requires process injection or admin rights. Defend with endpoint monitoring, least privilege, updates, application controls, physical inspection where appropriate, and phishing-resistant authentication. Transport encryption alone cannot secure a compromised endpoint. Phishing is an important delivery route in the lab context: a deceptive attachment or download may install a software keylogger. Other routes include compromised software, exploitation, and physical installation of hardware. A cloned login page captures submitted credentials directly and does not require a keylogger. Physical access controls address hardware capture; endpoint controls address malicious software.
questions.teach: Protection during transmission does not protect the moment data is typed on a compromised device.
questions.example: The lab’s isolated victim records test keystrokes. An organization should investigate the endpoint and account access rather than assume HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) prevented disclosure.
questions.correct: The endpoint can capture keystrokes before transport encryption

All keyloggers are network routers

questions.title: Hardening and patch workflow
questions.q: What belongs in OS hardening and a safe patch rollout?
questions.answer: Inventory assets, apply tested updates, use standard-user accounts, remove unnecessary services, enable appropriate endpoint firewall and protection, restrict software execution, and monitor changes. A patch workflow downloads, tests, pilots, schedules, deploys, and verifies, with rollback planning. NAC (Network Access Control) checks access posture; GPO (Group Policy Object) distributes domain policy. Patching addresses known vulnerabilities but does not eliminate zero-days. Legacy tool names in notes are historical examples, not a current shopping list. Use a standard non-administrator account for routine work and elevate only for approved tasks. Maintain an asset inventory, remove unnecessary software, disable unneeded services, restrict exposed ports, configure host firewalls, keep antivirus/EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) current, and enable appropriate automatic updates. Test and stage changes where needed, verify installation, and monitor failures. An antivirus detects known or suspicious malicious content; EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) adds investigation telemetry and response capabilities.
questions.teach: Reduce attack surface and limit damage before an incident. Verify that deployed controls actually work.
questions.example: A business tests a browser update in a representative VM (Virtual Machine), deploys to a pilot group, monitors compatibility, then expands rollout.
questions.correct: Test updates, reduce services and privileges, enforce controls, and verify

Allow daily work with administrator rights

questions.title: Visibility and incident interpretation
questions.q: How should an analyst interpret an attack timeline?
questions.answer: Correlate host process events, network connections, authentication logs, and file changes. A SOC (Security Operations Center) coordinates monitoring and response. EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) supplies endpoint detection and response evidence. Reconnaissance gathers information; privilege escalation increases rights; credential dumping extracts stored authentication material; SMB (Server Message Block) commonly supports network file sharing. Process hollowing replaces or maps malicious code into another process context. PowerShell is an administration shell and scripting environment; a sandbox is an isolated execution environment. DLL (Dynamic Link Library) means Dynamic Link Library. Infiltration gains entry; exfiltration removes information. For a business explanation, connect the sequence to impact: initial access may expose accounts; privilege escalation expands access; credential dumping can enable impersonation; process hollowing can conceal execution; C2 (Command and Control) carries remote instructions; exfiltration removes data. Correlate identity, process, file, and network evidence. The SOC (Security Operations Center) investigates and coordinates containment; EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) can expose process ancestry and support endpoint isolation. A penetration test demonstrates a weakness and its potential consequences; it does not by itself prove a real breach occurred.
questions.teach: Separate the tools, techniques, evidence, and outcomes. Seeing a tool name alone does not establish malicious intent.
questions.example: An Office process starts unusual PowerShell, followed by a new outbound connection and credential access. Build a timeline, identify affected hosts, preserve evidence, and contain according to the incident plan.
questions.correct: Correlate process, network, identity, and file evidence into a timeline
distractors: Treat all PowerShell use as proof of compromise
Sandbox means the same as PowerShell
Exfiltration means installing a software update
