questions.title: Lab 0 and isolation
questions.q: What do the VirtualBox network adapters and snapshots contribute to safe testing?
questions.answer: The host runs VirtualBox and the guest operating systems. The lab uses Kali and Windows 7 guests with an internal network for guest-to-guest tests and NAT (Network Address Translation) for controlled Internet access during setup. Internal networking does not make the entire host immune; additional adapters and sharing features affect exposure. Static guest addresses support predictable connectivity. Snapshots help restore a known lab state but do not replace independent backups. Disabling a guest firewall was an intentionally weakened lab condition, not a production hardening practice.
questions.teach: Explain why a control is disabled in a demonstration and why a real organization would enforce it.
questions.example: A tester uses an isolated guest network to observe activity, takes a baseline snapshot, and restores the guest after the exercise.
questions.correct: Isolation and reproducible guest states support controlled testing
distractors: NAT and internal network are identical
A snapshot replaces every backup
Disabling production firewalls is a hardening step
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Lab 0 and isolation in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: NAT and internal network are identical

setting.object: A student runs intentionally vulnerable guest machines for a controlled lab.
setting.location: Virtualization software, guest operating systems, virtual network adapters, and saved states.
setting.purpose: Keep experiments controlled and distinguish the guest environment from the physical host.
setting.action: Hypervisors manage guests; network settings affect reachability; snapshots help restore states. Containers, VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure), and uncontrolled VM (Virtual Machine) growth have different boundaries and management concerns.
setting.example: A tester uses an isolated guest network to observe activity, takes a baseline snapshot, and restores the guest after the exercise.

questions.title: Suspicious website analysis
questions.q: How do static, dynamic, and reputation checks complement each other?
questions.answer: Static work inspects HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), scripts, redirects, and embedded references without execution. Dynamic work observes behavior in an isolated environment, including processes, files, registry, and traffic. Reputation checks compare against previous reports. Automation is fast but can miss new threats; manual investigation provides context but takes skill and time. A legitimate site can be compromised. Firebug, Malzilla, Wepawet, JSUnpack, SiteAdvisor, and Safe Web are course-era examples.
questions.teach: A known domain and a clean reputation report are evidence, not guarantees.
questions.example: A site’s source includes a hidden redirect. An analyst reviews it, consults reputation evidence, and examines behavior in an approved sandbox.
questions.correct: Combine source inspection, isolated behavior observation, and reputation evidence
distractors: A familiar brand proves a page is safe
Automated always means static
A clean reputation scan proves no new malware exists
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Suspicious website analysis in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A familiar brand proves a page is safe

setting.object: An analyst examines a suspicious web page and its scripts.
setting.location: Page source, an isolated test browser, and website-analysis services.
setting.purpose: Determine what the page does and interpret the evidence behind a safety rating.
setting.action: Static analysis inspects without executing; dynamic analysis observes execution. Manual and automated describe who performs the work; reputation summarizes observations.
setting.example: A site’s source includes a hidden redirect. An analyst reviews it, consults reputation evidence, and examines behavior in an approved sandbox.

questions.title: Hash encryption and signatures
questions.q: Which cryptographic operation should you use for secrecy, comparison, or signed origin?
questions.answer: Encryption protects content confidentiality and is reversible with the correct key. Hashing produces a deterministic fixed-length digest with no intended inverse. A signature uses a private signing key and is checked with a corresponding public key to authenticate authorized data and detect alteration. A bare hash has no secret and does not prove origin. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) combines a secret key and hash for integrity and shared-key authentication; it is not encryption and does not provide the same public verification as a signature.
questions.teach: Choose the operation by the required property rather than calling every cryptographic output ciphertext.
questions.example: A document can be hashed for comparison, signed to show approval, and encrypted for its intended reader. These operations have separate roles.
questions.correct: Encrypt for secrecy, hash for comparison, sign for verifiable authorization
distractors: Decrypt SHA-256 to recover the message
Use a bare hash to prove sender identity
Signing automatically encrypts the whole document
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Hash encryption and signatures in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Decrypt SHA-256 to recover the message

setting.object: A business sends a private document and needs to detect changes or verify its approval.
setting.location: The document, any encrypted representation, its computed digest, and any digital signature.
setting.purpose: Choose the operation that fits confidentiality, content comparison, or origin verification.
setting.action: Encryption hides readable content; a trusted hash comparison checks content; a signature supports verification under a trusted signing key. These operations are not interchangeable.
setting.example: A document can be hashed for comparison, signed to show approval, and encrypted for its intended reader. These operations have separate roles.

questions.title: Symmetric and asymmetric keys
questions.q: Which keys protect a message for Bob and allow Bob to verify Alice’s signature?
questions.answer: Symmetric encryption shares one secret for encryption and decryption and is efficient for bulk data. Public-key encryption uses the recipient’s public key and recipient’s private key to decrypt. Signing uses the sender’s private key and verification uses the sender’s public key. Verify the binding between a public key and a claimed identity. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is symmetric; RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) belong to asymmetric families. DES and 3DES are historical course examples, not preferred new-system choices.
questions.teach: For confidentiality, use the recipient’s public encryption key so the recipient’s private key can decrypt. For a signature, the sender uses the sender’s private signing key; others verify with the corresponding trusted public key. The private keys remain secret.
questions.example: Alice wants only Bob to read a message and wants Bob to verify her approval. She protects it for Bob and signs it using her own signing key.
questions.correct: Encrypt for Bob using Bob’s public key; Alice signs using her private key, and Bob verifies using Alice’s trusted public key.
distractors: Encrypt with sender public key for only Bob to read
Share all private keys for authentication
Use receiver private key on the sender’s machine
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Symmetric and asymmetric keys in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Encrypt with sender public key for only Bob to read
questions.originalPrompt: Whose key does a sender use for confidentiality, and whose for a signature?

setting.object: Alice sends Bob a confidential document and may also sign it.
setting.location: Alice’s and Bob’s applications, cryptographic keys, the document, and any signature.
setting.purpose: Keep the contents readable by the intended recipient and independently verify signed content.
setting.action: Public-key encryption for Bob uses Bob’s public key and corresponding private decryption key. Alice signs with her private signing key; verification uses her trusted public key. Hybrid systems combine public-key techniques with symmetric data protection.
setting.example: Alice wants only Bob to read a message and wants Bob to verify her approval. She protects it for Bob and signs it using her own signing key.

questions.title: RSA arithmetic
questions.q: How does the classroom RSA example connect public and private exponents?
questions.answer: For distinct primes p and q, n=pq and φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1). Choose e with gcd(e,φ(n))=1 and choose d so ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n). Textbook notation may use m for φ(n). Classroom encryption is c=m^e mod n and decryption is m=c^d mod n. With p=5, q=11, n=55, φ=40, e=3, d=27: message 7 gives ciphertext 13 and decrypts to 7. The notes’ condition using e and n is incorrect; coprimality with φ(n) is essential. Small unpadded examples teach arithmetic and are not secure deployments.
questions.teach: The private exponent reverses the public exponent modulo n for correctly constructed RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman). Real implementations require safe key sizes and padding.
questions.example: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7.
questions.correct: Choose e coprime to φ(n), then d as its modular inverse
distractors: Choose e equal to φ(n)
Use addition instead of modular exponentiation
Make d public and hide e
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) arithmetic in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Choose e equal to φ(n)

setting.object: A classroom program encrypts and decrypts a small integer using a toy RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) example.
setting.location: The program’s selected primes, modulus, exponents, and modular calculations.
setting.purpose: Understand the mathematical relationship between public and private exponents.
setting.action: Choose e coprime to φ(n), and d so ed leaves remainder one modulo φ(n). The small unpadded example teaches arithmetic and is not suitable for real confidential data.
setting.example: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7.

questions.title: Nonce Merkle root and tampering
questions.q: What separate jobs do a proof-of-work nonce, a Merkle root, and the previous-block hash perform?
questions.answer: A proof-of-work nonce is a value miners vary while searching for a block-header hash meeting a target. A Merkle root commits to the block’s transactions using a tree of hashes. The previous-block hash links a block to its predecessor. Altering a transaction changes its commitment and invalidates later links unless recomputed. A toy rehash demonstration is not the full security model: distributed validation and cumulative proof of work make rewriting accepted history difficult.
questions.teach: A nonce is a search value. The Merkle root is computed from transaction hashes. The previous-block hash identifies the earlier block being built upon. These values support different parts of the block structure.
questions.example: Changing one transaction changes the Merkle root, then its block header hash and the descendants’ required links.
questions.correct: The nonce is varied to search for a qualifying hash; the Merkle root summarizes the transactions; the previous-block hash links to earlier history.
distractors: Nonce is the receiver’s private key
Merkle root stores every private password
Prior hash encrypts all previous transactions
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Nonce Merkle root and tampering in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Nonce is the receiver’s private key
questions.originalPrompt: What do a nonce, Merkle root, and previous-block hash do?

setting.object: A block records transactions and points to earlier blockchain history.
setting.location: Transaction hashes, the Merkle tree, block-header fields, and the previous-block hash.
setting.purpose: Summarize included transactions and make changes to linked history detectable.
setting.action: A Merkle root commits to transactions; a proof checks inclusion under that root. The previous-block hash links history; a proof-of-work nonce is varied during the mining search.
setting.example: Changing one transaction changes the Merkle root, then its block header hash and the descendants’ required links.

questions.title: Bitcoin incentives privacy and double spending
questions.q: Why use signatures, incentives, and consensus together in Bitcoin?
questions.answer: Signatures demonstrate authorization to spend. Nodes check spending rules, including whether an output is unspent. Consensus orders transactions so competing spends do not both become accepted history. A block subsidy and fees incentivize miners. Public records use addresses or spending scripts rather than mandatory civil identities, but linked transactions can reveal relationships. This is pseudonymity. Nakamoto’s paper contrasts verification by cryptographic proof with the reversal costs, mediation, and trust demands of financial intermediaries.
questions.teach: Authorization does not establish which of two conflicting authorized spends came first; network agreement addresses that ordering problem.
questions.example: An owner attempts to spend the same output twice. Both signatures could be valid, but both transactions cannot be accepted in one valid history.
questions.correct: Signatures authorize, consensus orders, and rewards motivate participation
distractors: Hashing alone prevents all double spending
All Bitcoin addresses guarantee anonymity
Miners can authorize spending anyone’s coins
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Bitcoin incentives privacy and double spending in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Hashing alone prevents all double spending

setting.object: A user transfers digital value to another user without a central ledger operator.
setting.location: Transactions and blocks validated by participating Bitcoin computers.
setting.purpose: Authorize spending, prevent conflicting accepted spends, and maintain an agreed history.
setting.action: Keys authorize spending through signatures; nodes validate transactions; consensus establishes accepted history; incentives support block production.
setting.example: An owner attempts to spend the same output twice. Both signatures could be valid, but both transactions cannot be accepted in one valid history.

questions.title: TCP UDP IP and handshake
questions.q: What different jobs do TCP, UDP, and IP perform when computers communicate?
questions.answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides a reliable ordered byte stream, using SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for conventional connection establishment. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides datagrams without TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)-style delivery or ordering guarantees and is useful where applications tolerate loss or implement their own recovery. Both operate at the transport layer. IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and routes packets at the network layer with best-effort delivery. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is not restricted to private networks, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does not guarantee timeliness or encryption. Packet lengths can vary. A network packet is a unit of data handled at the network layer, not the smallest possible unit of transmission. Its header contains addressing and control fields; its payload (body) carries the data, including higher-layer headers. Bits, link-layer frames, IP (Internet Protocol) packets, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segments name different units. A TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reverse shell uses TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) for the outbound shell connection; TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reliability does not make that connection trustworthy.
questions.teach: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) puts received bytes in order and retransmits missing data when possible. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sends individual messages called datagrams without automatically recovering missing messages or putting them in order. IP (Internet Protocol) handles addressing and forwarding packets between networks; best effort means it does not promise delivery.
questions.example: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP (Internet Protocol) routing.
questions.correct: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP sends separate messages without those guarantees; IP forwards packets toward destinations.
distractors: IP guarantees every byte in order
UDP is only allowed on private networks
TCP stands for Transportation Control Protocol
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) UDP (User Datagram Protocol) IP (Internet Protocol) and handshake in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: IP guarantees every byte in order
questions.originalPrompt: How do TCP, UDP, and IP differ, and what is the TCP handshake?

setting.object: A laptop sends file data to a server across a network.
setting.location: The application, transport service, IP (Internet Protocol) network, and local links.
setting.purpose: Understand which layer handles reliable delivery, separate messages, and forwarding.
setting.action: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides separate datagrams without those guarantees; IP (Internet Protocol) forwards packets toward destinations.
setting.example: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP (Internet Protocol) routing.

questions.title: Network administration protocols
questions.q: Which statement correctly matches DNS, SNMP, ICMP, FTP, SMTP, and POP to their jobs?
questions.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names and other records; poisoning supplies false resolution information. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) authenticates signed DNS (Domain Name System) data and integrity when correctly validated, without encrypting ordinary DNS (Domain Name System) queries. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) monitors and manages devices; v3 supports stronger protection. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) carries network control and diagnostic messages, including ping. Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transfers files without encryption: port 21 controls, port 20 is traditionally active-mode data, while passive mode negotiates data ports. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail and POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves it. Wireshark analyzes packets; log correlation helps investigation.
questions.teach: Each protocol defines rules for a different communication task. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) adds authentication of signed DNS (Domain Name System) data, not encryption of ordinary queries. Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) does not encrypt its transfers. A protocol’s name alone does not mean its traffic is confidential.
questions.example: A name resolves unexpectedly, so an analyst checks DNS (Domain Name System) evidence and validation. Separate authentication logs and packet metadata help establish the incident timeline.
questions.correct: DNS looks up names; SNMP manages devices; ICMP carries network diagnostic/control messages; FTP transfers files; SMTP sends mail; POP retrieves mail.
distractors: DNSSEC encrypts every website
FTP always uses port 20 for all traffic
ICMP is a mail retrieval service
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Network administration protocols in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: DNSSEC encrypts every website
questions.originalPrompt: What do DNS, DNSSEC, SNMP, ICMP, FTP, SMTP, and POP contribute?

setting.object: A computer looks up a mail server, sends a message, and retrieves mail.
setting.location: The client, DNS (Domain Name System) service, mail servers, and network connections.
setting.purpose: Distinguish the communication jobs performed by different protocols.
setting.action: DNS (Domain Name System) looks up names; SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail; POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves mail. TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) is a family of cooperating protocols.
setting.example: A name resolves unexpectedly, so an analyst checks DNS (Domain Name System) evidence and validation. Separate authentication logs and packet metadata help establish the incident timeline.

questions.title: Spoofing and captive portals
questions.q: Why are SSIDs, IP addresses, and captive portals insufficient proof of trust?
questions.answer: Spoofing impersonates an identifier such as an address or caller identity. An evil-twin wireless access point can imitate a familiar SSID and lure users; a Wi-Fi assessment device can demonstrate these risks but cannot automatically decrypt all nearby secure traffic. A captive portal presents network-access or acceptance steps; its appearance alone does not establish legitimacy. Verify the network and destination, and use authenticated secure protocols.
questions.teach: A familiar name is easy to copy. Trust requires verification beyond a displayed label.
questions.example: A traveler sees two access points with the hotel’s name. The name alone cannot determine which is authorized.
questions.correct: Displayed names and addresses can be impersonated
distractors: Every matching SSID proves the same operator
A portal guarantees encrypted traffic
A Wi-Fi gadget automatically decrypts TLS
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Spoofing and captive portals in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every matching SSID proves the same operator

setting.object: A traveler sees a wireless network name that looks like the hotel’s network.
setting.location: The Wi-Fi selection screen, access point, and any captive login page.
setting.purpose: Avoid treating a copied name or convincing page as proof of a trusted operator.
setting.action: Displayed names and identifiers can be spoofed. Verify the intended network and service rather than relying on the familiar label alone.
setting.example: A traveler sees two access points with the hotel’s name. The name alone cannot determine which is authorized.

questions.title: Chapter 3 overview and study route
questions.q: Which Chapter 3 protection best addresses a lost, powered-off laptop containing confidential files?
questions.answer: Steganography hides the existence of data; encryption hides readable content. ROT13 is a substitution cipher, and XOR gives 0 for equal input bits and 1 for different bits. Stream ciphers process streams; block ciphers process fixed-size blocks. Diffusion spreads a plaintext change through the output; confusion obscures the relation between key and ciphertext. Secure randomness and key management matter. Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret; ephemeral exchanges can support forward secrecy when used correctly. Downgrade attacks force weaker options. TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and HSM (Hardware Security Module) protect cryptographic operations and keys; full-disk encryption protects stored data. Resource, power, and latency constraints influence implementation choices.
questions.teach: Full-disk encryption protects data saved on the drive. It does not prevent every attack after the device is unlocked. Other Chapter 3 concepts have separate definition questions, including steganography, forward secrecy, TPM (Trusted Platform Module), HSM (Hardware Security Module), and stream and block ciphers.
questions.example: A lost powered-off encrypted laptop needs storage protection. A compromised running session exposes data in use, so disk encryption alone is insufficient.
questions.correct: Full-disk encryption protects stored data when the keys remain protected.
distractors: Steganography always encrypts content
A TPM prevents every software exploit
Forward secrecy means keys never change
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
questions.goal: Explain Chapter 3 overview and study route in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Steganography always encrypts content
questions.originalPrompt: What additional Chapter 3 concepts should you recognize?

setting.object: A laptop holds sensitive files, and some may be open in applications.
setting.location: Stored drive data, files in working memory, and key-protection components.
setting.purpose: Match protection to stored data, traveling data, or data currently being used.
setting.action: File or disk encryption protects selected stored contents. TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and HSM (Hardware Security Module) protect particular keys and operations. An unlocked application can still expose readable information.
setting.example: A lost powered-off encrypted laptop needs storage protection. A compromised running session exposes data in use, so disk encryption alone is insufficient.

questions.title: Why attacks succeed
questions.q: How do vulnerable software, configuration, resource limits, and business processes create different weaknesses?
questions.teach: A flaw can exist in the product, in its settings, in its limited capacity, or in the way people do business. Fixing one category does not automatically fix another.
questions.answer: Chapter 1 groups weaknesses into widespread vulnerabilities, configuration issues, poor software design, hardware limitations, and enterprise issues. Unsupported or end-of-life products may lack patches. Default settings and excessive account privileges are configuration issues. Unsafe input, error handling, and races are design issues. Resource exhaustion consumes CPU (Central Processing Unit), memory, storage, or connections. Business-process compromise manipulates legitimate workflows; undocumented assets create system sprawl. Defenses include inventory, supported software, hardened settings, safe design, capacity controls, and verification of unusual business requests.
questions.example: A patched accounting system still processes a fraudulent payment because staff skip the callback check. This is a process weakness even though the software is up to date.
questions.correct: Different weakness categories require different controls
distractors: Patching fixes every process weakness
All successful attacks require a zero-day
More bandwidth fixes excessive user privileges
questions.goal: Explain Why attacks succeed in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Patching fixes every process weakness

setting.object: A company discovers an unpatched server, an unsafe setting, and a fraudulent payment request.
setting.location: Software, device configuration, limited system resources, and business procedures.
setting.purpose: Identify which kind of weakness permits each kind of harm.
setting.action: Patching repairs software flaws; secure settings restrict exposure; capacity controls address exhaustion; verification procedures address deceptive business requests.
setting.example: A patched accounting system still processes a fraudulent payment because staff skip the callback check. This is a process weakness even though the software is up to date.

questions.title: Asset threat vulnerability and vector
questions.q: How do an asset, a vulnerability, a threat, and risk relate in a security decision?
questions.teach: An asset is something valuable. A vulnerability is a weakness. A threat is a potential cause of harm. Risk considers how likely harm is and how serious it would be. An attack vector is the route used to reach the target.
questions.answer: An asset is something valuable. A threat is potential harm; a threat actor can cause that harm. A vulnerability is a weakness. An attack vector is a route or means of attack; the attack surface includes the collection of exposed opportunities. Risk concerns potential loss in context, including likelihood and impact. A threat is not proof an incident occurred. Reducing unnecessary services can shrink attack surface, while fixing a flaw removes a particular vulnerability.
questions.example: A student database is the asset, data theft is the threat, a criminal is the actor, an unpatched web application is the weakness, and the exposed application is an attack route.
questions.correct: A valuable resource has a weakness; something could exploit it; risk considers the likelihood and impact of the resulting harm.
distractors: Asset and threat always mean the same thing
An attack vector is the attacker’s salary
Every threat is already a successful breach
questions.goal: Explain Asset threat vulnerability and vector in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Asset and threat always mean the same thing
questions.originalPrompt: How do asset, threat, threat actor, vulnerability, attack vector, attack surface, and risk connect?

setting.object: A school stores private student records and operates a registration service.
setting.location: The records, accounts, applications, and computers used by students and staff.
setting.purpose: Protect privacy, accurate records, and usable services while assessing likely harm.
setting.action: Identify valuable assets, weaknesses, possible threats, and likelihood and impact. Reduce, avoid, accept, or transfer risk according to the action taken.
setting.example: A student database is the asset, data theft is the threat, a criminal is the actor, an unpatched web application is the weakness, and the exposed application is an attack route.

questions.title: Risk response choices
questions.q: A business installs a patch to reduce a known security risk. Which risk response is it using?
questions.teach: Mitigate means reduce. A patch repairs a weakness, reducing the chance of a successful attack. Acceptance means knowingly living with risk; avoidance means stopping the risky activity; transfer shifts some consequences, such as through insurance.
questions.answer: Accepting risk acknowledges exposure under a deliberate decision. Avoidance stops the risky activity. Transfer shifts some financial consequences through insurance or an appropriate agreement; it does not remove all responsibility. Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact through controls. Deterrence discourages attackers. A course expression such as threat × vulnerability × cost is a conceptual aid, not a measured probability formula unless its variables are defined.
questions.example: For a risky remote service, canceling it is avoidance; adding MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) is mitigation; buying suitable insurance transfers some loss; documenting a tolerable residual exposure is acceptance.
questions.correct: Mitigation: reducing the likelihood or impact of harm.
distractors: Buying insurance patches software
Accept means the risk was eliminated
Mitigate means never using the service
questions.goal: Explain Risk response choices in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Buying insurance patches software
questions.originalPrompt: How can you distinguish accepting, avoiding, transferring, and mitigating risk?

setting.object: A school stores private student records and operates a registration service.
setting.location: The records, accounts, applications, and computers used by students and staff.
setting.purpose: Protect privacy, accurate records, and usable services while assessing likely harm.
setting.action: Identify valuable assets, weaknesses, possible threats, and likelihood and impact. Reduce, avoid, accept, or transfer risk according to the action taken.
setting.example: For a risky remote service, canceling it is avoidance; adding MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) is mitigation; buying suitable insurance transfers some loss; documenting a tolerable residual exposure is acceptance.

questions.title: People products and procedures
questions.q: Why can a security product fail without people and procedures?
questions.teach: A tool needs someone to configure and use it, and a repeatable procedure for acting on what it finds.
questions.answer: The textbook’s layers are products, people, and policies/procedures. Products include technical and physical safeguards. People configure and use them. Procedures define approved actions and escalation. Technical controls use technology, administrative controls guide behavior, and physical controls restrict physical access. Security must support useful business work; inconvenient controls may cause workarounds. Compliance is one requirement, not proof that attacks cannot succeed.
questions.example: A sensor produces alerts, but no one owns the review queue. Buying another sensor does not solve the missing monitoring responsibility.
questions.correct: Tools, responsible people, and defined procedures must work together
distractors: A product automatically creates an incident process
Only IT staff affect security
Every compliant system is immune to attack
questions.goal: Explain People products and procedures in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A product automatically creates an incident process

setting.object: A store separates payment computers, checks incoming traffic, records device activity, and provides backup network equipment.
setting.location: Network boundaries, staff computers, security records, and the people managing controls.
setting.purpose: Keep the business operating while restricting harmful actions at multiple points.
setting.action: Layer complementary controls, grant necessary access only, collect useful evidence, and plan for growth and device failure. People and procedures must support the tools.
setting.example: A sensor produces alerts, but no one owns the review queue. Buying another sensor does not solve the missing monitoring responsibility.

questions.title: Threat actor attributes
questions.q: Which facts help assess what a threat actor can do and why they might do it?
questions.teach: Capability means skills and tools. Resources include money and time. Access describes what the actor can already reach. Motivation is the reason for acting. A trusted employee and an outside criminal may have different opportunities even when both want money.
questions.answer: Compare sophistication, funding/resources, internal versus external position, and intent. Script kiddies use existing tools; hacktivists pursue ideological goals; criminals pursue gain; competitors may steal valuable research; brokers sell vulnerability knowledge; nation-state actors may conduct sustained espionage. APT (Advanced Persistent Threat) describes sustained targeted activity, often associated with state actors. Insiders include employees, contractors, and partners. Assess behaviors and evidence rather than assuming nationality or a single label proves intent.
questions.example: An insider can export customer records through ordinary access, while a well-funded external group can patiently target a specific research system.
questions.correct: Their skills, money and tools, existing access, and motivation.
distractors: All insiders have malicious intent
Only experts can use attack tools
A zero-day is a category of employee
questions.goal: Explain Threat actor attributes in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: All insiders have malicious intent
questions.originalPrompt: How do capability, resources, access, and motivation change threat assessment?

setting.object: A company considers both a malicious employee and an outside criminal group.
setting.location: The organization’s accounts, information, services, and existing access.
setting.purpose: Assess what each actor could reach, why they might act, and what resources they have.
setting.action: Compare motivation, capability, resources, and access instead of assuming every attacker has the same opportunities.
setting.example: An insider can export customer records through ordinary access, while a well-funded external group can patiently target a specific research system.

questions.title: Roles and fundamental principles
questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches a security role with its duties?
questions.teach: In this textbook, the security administrator analyzes and designs solutions for users. A technician installs, configures, and troubleshoots tools. A manager supervises personnel. Layering, limiting, diversity, obscurity, and simplicity are separate principles, each with its own definition question.
questions.answer: In this textbook the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) leads security, the manager supervises staff, the administrator manages daily technology and analyzes/designs solutions, and the technician configures and troubleshoots. Layering adds barriers; limiting grants necessary rights; diversity reduces common failure modes; obscurity conceals unnecessary details; simplicity keeps defenses manageable. Vendor diversity alone does not guarantee independence, and secrecy alone does not establish security.
questions.example: An administrator chooses a combination of access rules and endpoint controls. A technician installs and troubleshoots them. A manager allocates staffing for monitoring.
questions.correct: An administrator designs solutions and identifies users’ needs; a technician configures tools; a manager supervises the team.
distractors: A technician and CISO always have identical duties
Using two identical rules guarantees diversity
Complexity always improves security
questions.goal: Explain Roles and fundamental principles in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A technician and CISO always have identical duties
questions.originalPrompt: How do security roles differ, and how do the five principles guide their decisions?

setting.purpose: Match a job’s actual duties to the textbook’s role definitions.
setting.action: The administrator designs solutions for users, the technician configures and troubleshoots tools, and the manager supervises personnel.
setting.example: An administrator chooses a combination of access rules and endpoint controls. A technician installs and troubleshoots them. A manager allocates staffing for monitoring.

questions.title: Why organizations protect information
questions.q: What business consequences make information security necessary?
questions.teach: Think beyond stolen files: a breach can impersonate customers, interrupt work, damage trust, and create reporting or contractual obligations.
questions.answer: Chapter 1 discusses data theft, identity theft, legal/compliance consequences, lost productivity, and cyberterrorism affecting critical services. For course recognition, HIPAA relates to protected health information, Sarbanes-Oxley to public-company financial reporting/internal controls, GLBA to financial-information privacy, and PCI DSS to payment-card security as an industry standard. These are category associations from the assigned text, not current legal advice. Do not memorize the old edition’s fines or notification deadlines as current facts.
questions.example: A stolen patient record affects privacy and trust. A service outage diverts staff from normal work. A company may also need to investigate obligations with appropriate specialists.
questions.correct: Security protects business continuity, information, identity, and trust
distractors: Only the replacement cost of hardware matters
PCI DSS is the same as a criminal statute
An unavailable system cannot cause business loss
questions.goal: Explain Why organizations protect information in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Only the replacement cost of hardware matters

setting.object: A school stores private student records and operates a registration service.
setting.location: The records, accounts, applications, and computers used by students and staff.
setting.purpose: Protect privacy, accurate records, and usable services while assessing likely harm.
setting.action: Identify valuable assets, weaknesses, possible threats, and likelihood and impact. Reduce, avoid, accept, or transfer risk according to the action taken.
setting.example: A stolen patient record affects privacy and trust. A service outage diverts staff from normal work. A company may also need to investigate obligations with appropriate specialists.

questions.title: Data at rest in transit and in use
questions.q: Which example correctly matches data at rest, in transit, and in use?
questions.teach: Different stages expose data in different places. Storage encryption protects stored data. Protected communication helps while it travels. Permissions and endpoint protection help when programs use readable data.
questions.answer: Data at rest is stored, such as a powered-off laptop’s files. Data in transit travels across a network. Data in use is being processed on an endpoint. Disk encryption helps against offline access; TLS (Transport Layer Security) protects a connection; endpoint controls and careful access restrictions protect use. Keys, recovery, trusted devices, and authentication matter in all cases. A keylogger exposes why encrypted transport cannot rescue plaintext already captured on the endpoint.
questions.example: A payroll file on disk, the same file being uploaded, and its contents open in a running application illustrate the three states.
questions.correct: A saved file is at rest; a message crossing a network is in transit; a document being processed by a program is in use.
distractors: TLS alone protects a stolen offline drive
Disk encryption prevents every keylogger
Data in use means only data crossing a router
questions.goal: Explain Data at rest in transit and in use in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: TLS alone protects a stolen offline drive
questions.originalPrompt: How does the state of data change the protection it needs?

setting.object: A laptop holds sensitive files, and some may be open in applications.
setting.location: Stored drive data, files in working memory, and key-protection components.
setting.purpose: Match protection to stored data, traveling data, or data currently being used.
setting.action: File or disk encryption protects selected stored contents. TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and HSM (Hardware Security Module) protect particular keys and operations. An unlocked application can still expose readable information.
setting.example: A payroll file on disk, the same file being uploaded, and its contents open in a running application illustrate the three states.

questions.title: Substitution ROT13 and XOR
questions.q: What do the simple ciphers teach, and what are their limits?
questions.teach: A substitution replaces symbols. ROT13 shifts letters by 13 positions. XOR compares bits: same gives 0 and different gives 1.
questions.answer: ROT13 applied twice recovers the original letters, demonstrating reversibility. XOR has the useful identity (message XOR key) XOR key = message. For example 1010 XOR 0110 = 1100, then 1100 XOR 0110 = 1010. These operations teach algorithms and keys. ROT13 has no meaningful secrecy against someone who knows the rule; repeating a short XOR key is not a secure replacement for a designed cryptographic scheme.
questions.example: Using the same XOR bit pattern twice cancels it. This is different from hashing, where there is no corresponding decryption step.
questions.correct: XOR returns 0 for equal bits and 1 for different bits
distractors: 1 XOR 1 equals 2
ROT13 is a one-way hash
XOR always gives 1
questions.goal: Explain Substitution ROT13 and XOR in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: 1 XOR 1 equals 2

setting.object: A program processes a message using a cryptographic construction.
setting.location: The message data, procedure, key material, and internal processing steps.
setting.purpose: Distinguish processing rules and security requirements instead of treating every construction as the same.
setting.action: Substitution replaces symbols; XOR combines bits; block and stream ciphers process data differently. Secure randomness, correct key use, confusion, and diffusion have distinct roles; a true one-time pad is never reused.
setting.example: Using the same XOR bit pattern twice cancels it. This is different from hashing, where there is no corresponding decryption step.

questions.title: Randomness confusion and diffusion
questions.q: Why do cryptographic randomness, confusion, and diffusion matter?
questions.teach: A secret key must be hard to predict. The output should not expose simple patterns linking the message and key.
questions.answer: Cryptographic randomness supplies unpredictable secrets. A PRNG is algorithmic and deterministic; a cryptographically secure generator must be designed and seeded appropriately. Diffusion spreads a plaintext change through output. Confusion complicates the relation between key and ciphertext. These frustrate pattern analysis, but do not excuse weak keys, implementation errors, or exposed secrets. An ordinary predictable random-number generator is not suitable simply because its output looks irregular.
questions.example: If every key is derived from the current minute, a strong cipher may still be easy to guess. Strong mathematics cannot compensate for predictable key generation.
questions.correct: Unpredictable secrets and hidden input/key patterns resist analysis
distractors: A hidden algorithm removes the need for keys
More randomness changes hash output length
Diffusion means packets arrive faster
questions.goal: Explain Randomness confusion and diffusion in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A hidden algorithm removes the need for keys

setting.object: A program processes a message using a cryptographic construction.
setting.location: The message data, procedure, key material, and internal processing steps.
setting.purpose: Distinguish processing rules and security requirements instead of treating every construction as the same.
setting.action: Substitution replaces symbols; XOR combines bits; block and stream ciphers process data differently. Secure randomness, correct key use, confusion, and diffusion have distinct roles; a true one-time pad is never reused.
setting.example: If every key is derived from the current minute, a strong cipher may still be easy to guess. Strong mathematics cannot compensate for predictable key generation.

questions.title: Stream block sponge and one-time pad
questions.q: How do a stream cipher, a block cipher, a sponge construction, and a one-time pad differ?
questions.teach: These are the four constructions in this question. A stream cipher processes data using a key-dependent stream. A block cipher operates on fixed-size blocks. A sponge absorbs input and squeezes output. A true one-time pad uses a random secret key as long as the message and never reuses it.
questions.answer: A stream cipher combines data with a keystream; a block cipher transforms fixed-size blocks under a key. Secure modes determine how blocks form a message. Sponge constructions absorb input and generate output; SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-3 uses this family of designs, while extendable-output variants can request different lengths. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) itself has a fixed-length digest. A true one-time pad requires a uniformly random secret key as long as the message, used once only. Reusing it destroys its special security. Stream ciphers are not inherently weaker than block ciphers.
questions.example: A short password repeated across a long file is not a one-time pad even if the program uses XOR.
questions.correct: Stream ciphers process a stream; block ciphers transform fixed-size blocks; sponge designs absorb then squeeze; a one-time pad needs a truly random key used once.
distractors: All stream ciphers are always insecure
SHA-256 produces any length requested
Any repeated password is a one-time pad
questions.goal: Explain Stream block sponge and one-time pad in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: All stream ciphers are always insecure
questions.originalPrompt: How do processing structure and key use distinguish these constructions?

setting.object: A program processes a message using a cryptographic construction.
setting.location: The message data, procedure, key material, and internal processing steps.
setting.purpose: Distinguish processing rules and security requirements instead of treating every construction as the same.
setting.action: Substitution replaces symbols; XOR combines bits; block and stream ciphers process data differently. Secure randomness, correct key use, confusion, and diffusion have distinct roles; a true one-time pad is never reused.
setting.example: A short password repeated across a long file is not a one-time pad even if the program uses XOR.

questions.title: Hashes HMAC and trusted comparisons
questions.q: What can a hash comparison establish, and what does HMAC add?
questions.teach: A plain hash is a fingerprint anyone can calculate. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) adds a secret shared by the parties, so unauthorized changes are harder to forge.
questions.answer: MD5, SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) families, and RIPEMD are hash families. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) outputs 256 bits, shown by 64 hexadecimal characters. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 have broken collision resistance. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) uses a hash and a secret key for message authentication/integrity; it does not encrypt. Both holders of a shared HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) key can produce a tag, so it is not a publicly verifiable proof of which holder acted. For download checking, the expected digest must come through a trusted channel. An attacker replacing a file and its untrusted posted hash defeats simple comparison.
questions.example: An analyst checks a downloaded file against an independently authenticated expected digest. A plain hash copied from the attacker’s page would not give the same assurance.
questions.correct: A trusted digest detects changes; HMAC adds shared-secret authentication
distractors: HMAC encrypts and hides the whole message
An untrusted posted hash proves authenticity
MD5 has guaranteed unique outputs
questions.goal: Explain Hashes HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) and trusted comparisons in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: HMAC encrypts and hides the whole message

setting.object: A downloaded file is compared with a publisher’s trusted reference digest.
setting.location: The file’s bytes and a program computing a digest from those bytes.
setting.purpose: Detect different contents using a trusted comparison, and distinguish that from sender authentication.
setting.action: A secure hash computes a fixed-length digest. Collisions remain possible but should be hard to find. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) additionally uses a shared secret for message authentication.
setting.example: An analyst checks a downloaded file against an independently authenticated expected digest. A plain hash copied from the attacker’s page would not give the same assurance.

questions.title: Symmetric algorithm recognition
questions.q: Which categories contain DES, 3DES, AES, RC4, Blowfish, Twofish, and IDEA?
questions.teach: Block ciphers transform fixed-size blocks. Stream ciphers process a key-dependent stream. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) uses 128-bit blocks with 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys. Recognizing a historical algorithm for the exam does not make it suitable for current use.
questions.answer: DES is a symmetric block cipher with a 56-bit key. 3DES applies the DES primitive three times; the two are historical course examples. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric block cipher with 128-bit blocks and keys of 128, 192, or 256 bits. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) total rounds are 10, 12, and 14 respectively; the textbook’s 9/11/13 count refers to its repeated middle-stage description, not the total standard rounds. RC4 is a historical stream cipher. Blowfish and Twofish are block ciphers; IDEA is also symmetric. Recognition is the study goal, not deploying every algorithm named in an old book.
questions.example: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)-256 uses a 256-bit key but still transforms 128-bit blocks. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) instead names a 256-bit hash digest.
questions.correct: DES, 3DES, AES, Blowfish, Twofish, and IDEA are symmetric block ciphers; RC4 is a symmetric stream cipher.
distractors: AES-256 always uses 256-bit blocks
RSA is a symmetric stream cipher
SHA-256 is AES with a different key
questions.goal: Explain Symmetric algorithm recognition in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: AES-256 always uses 256-bit blocks
questions.originalPrompt: How do DES, 3DES, AES, RC4, Blowfish, Twofish, and IDEA fit the categories?

setting.purpose: Distinguish processing rules and security requirements instead of treating every construction as the same.
setting.action: Substitution replaces symbols; XOR combines bits; block and stream ciphers process data differently. Secure randomness, correct key use, confusion, and diffusion have distinct roles; a true one-time pad is never reused.
setting.example: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)-256 uses a 256-bit key but still transforms 128-bit blocks. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) instead names a 256-bit hash digest.

questions.title: Key distribution and hybrid encryption
questions.q: Why do secure communication systems often combine asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
questions.teach: Asymmetric methods use a public/private key pair. Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret. Combining them avoids using expensive public-key operations for every byte of a large transfer. The parties must also authenticate the exchange.
questions.answer: In hybrid encryption, a fresh symmetric session key protects bulk data. A suitable public-key scheme protects that session key for the recipient, or an authenticated key agreement establishes it. The receiver uses the appropriate private-key capability to recover or derive the session secret, then decrypts the bulk data. PGP is the textbook example. Public keys still need trusted identity binding. The sender’s private key is not sent to the receiver, and public-key encryption alone does not authenticate who sent the message.
questions.example: A file is encrypted under a random session key. Only the intended recipient can recover that key from the protected key material and open the file.
questions.correct: Public-key techniques help establish or protect a shared secret; symmetric encryption efficiently protects the message data.
distractors: Send the recipient your private key
Encrypt every byte with an untrusted posted public key
Hash the file and call it encrypted
questions.goal: Explain Key distribution and hybrid encryption in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Send the recipient your private key
questions.originalPrompt: Why combine symmetric and asymmetric cryptography?

setting.object: Alice sends Bob a confidential document and may also sign it.
setting.location: Alice’s and Bob’s applications, cryptographic keys, the document, and any signature.
setting.purpose: Keep the contents readable by the intended recipient and independently verify signed content.
setting.action: Public-key encryption for Bob uses Bob’s public key and corresponding private decryption key. Alice signs with her private signing key; verification uses her trusted public key. Hybrid systems combine public-key techniques with symmetric data protection.
setting.example: A file is encrypted under a random session key. Only the intended recipient can recover that key from the protected key material and open the file.

questions.title: RSA ECC signatures and key exchange
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes RSA, ECC, digital signatures, and Diffie-Hellman?
questions.teach: RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) are mathematical foundations for particular schemes. Signatures let a recipient verify that the trusted signing key authorized specific content. Diffie-Hellman helps establish shared key material, but the exchange also needs authentication against impersonation.
questions.answer: RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) uses arithmetic related to large primes and supports suitable encryption/signature schemes. ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) is a family using elliptic-curve mathematics and can support signatures or agreement with different constructions. DSA is a signature algorithm, not bulk-data encryption. Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret; it does not by itself authenticate who participated. Ephemeral DH/ECDH can support forward secrecy so later long-term key compromise does not reveal properly established past sessions. Do not infer that every use of DH is static or every public-key algorithm has forward secrecy.
questions.example: A secure protocol authenticates the parties and establishes a fresh session secret, then uses efficient symmetric encryption for the conversation.
questions.correct: RSA and ECC support public-key constructions; signatures verify signed messages; Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret.
distractors: Diffie-Hellman alone proves civil identity
DSA is a disk-encryption mode
All RSA use automatically provides forward secrecy
questions.goal: Explain RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) signatures and key exchange in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Diffie-Hellman alone proves civil identity
questions.originalPrompt: What distinct jobs do RSA, ECC, signatures, and Diffie-Hellman perform?

setting.object: Alice sends Bob a confidential document and may also sign it.
setting.location: Alice’s and Bob’s applications, cryptographic keys, the document, and any signature.
setting.purpose: Keep the contents readable by the intended recipient and independently verify signed content.
setting.action: Public-key encryption for Bob uses Bob’s public key and corresponding private decryption key. Alice signs with her private signing key; verification uses her trusted public key. Hybrid systems combine public-key techniques with symmetric data protection.
setting.example: A secure protocol authenticates the parties and establishes a fresh session secret, then uses efficient symmetric encryption for the conversation.

questions.title: Signature verification from start to finish
questions.q: What does a recipient actually check when verifying a signed message?
questions.teach: The signature must match both the message and the trusted sender key. Verifying a signature is different from decrypting a message for privacy.
questions.answer: The sender signs a representation of the message using a private signing key. The recipient verifies the signature with a trusted corresponding public key and the received message. Alteration makes verification fail under the scheme’s assumptions. Signatures support origin authentication, integrity, and evidence of authorization/non-repudiation, subject to key custody and identity trust. A valid signature proves a key authorized the signed content; it does not automatically prove the content is true or secret. The textbook’s encrypted-digest diagram is a teaching model, not a universal implementation of every signature algorithm.
questions.example: Alice signs an invoice. If an attacker changes the amount, Bob’s verification fails. If Bob instead trusts an attacker’s substitute public key, he has not authenticated Alice.
questions.correct: Verify the received message and signature using the trusted sender public key
distractors: Decrypt the message with the sender public key to guarantee secrecy
Compare two untrusted plain hashes only
Use the recipient private key to identify the sender
questions.goal: Explain Signature verification from start to finish in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Decrypt the message with the sender public key to guarantee secrecy

setting.purpose: Keep the contents readable by the intended recipient and independently verify signed content.
setting.action: Public-key encryption for Bob uses Bob’s public key and corresponding private decryption key. Alice signs with her private signing key; verification uses her trusted public key. Hybrid systems combine public-key techniques with symmetric data protection.
setting.example: Alice signs an invoice. If an attacker changes the amount, Bob’s verification fails. If Bob instead trusts an attacker’s substitute public key, he has not authenticated Alice.

questions.title: Attacks on cryptography
questions.q: Which example distinguishes a downgrade attack from a weak algorithm or an implementation flaw?
questions.teach: An attacker can exploit the selected protocol, the mathematical protection, or the code that implements it. These are different problems: choosing a good algorithm does not automatically make flawed software safe.
questions.answer: Ciphertext-only analysis looks for useful patterns without the plaintext. A downgrade pushes a protocol into weaker settings. Deprecated algorithms have known weaknesses or no longer provide an adequate margin. Misconfiguration or implementation mistakes can expose keys, misuse randomness, or apply a primitive incorrectly. Collision attacks seek two matching-digest inputs; preimage attacks seek input for a particular digest. The birthday bound for an ideal n-bit digest is roughly 2^(n/2), distinct from a roughly 2^n generic preimage search.
questions.example: A strong encryption algorithm does not help if its key is bundled in a public file. That failure concerns key handling rather than breaking the cipher mathematically.
questions.correct: A downgrade forces a weaker option; a weak algorithm has inadequate protection; an implementation flaw is a mistake in the program using it.
distractors: Every cryptographic incident means AES was mathematically broken
A downgrade always improves protection
Collision and preimage searches are identical
questions.goal: Explain Attacks on cryptography in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every cryptographic incident means AES was mathematically broken
questions.originalPrompt: How do ciphertext analysis, downgrade, weak algorithms, and bad implementation differ?

setting.object: A device must protect communication while operating with limited memory, power, and response time.
setting.location: The implemented protocol, algorithm, software, and device resources.
setting.purpose: Provide appropriate security without ignoring implementation errors or operating limits.
setting.action: Weak algorithms, forced weaker settings, and programming mistakes create different problems. Resource limits affect implementation choices but do not justify assuming insecure choices are safe.
setting.example: A strong encryption algorithm does not help if its key is bundled in a public file. That failure concerns key handling rather than breaking the cipher mathematically.

questions.title: File encryption full-disk encryption and hardware
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes file encryption, full-disk encryption, TPM, and HSM?
questions.teach: Choose the protection according to where exposure occurs. A lost locked drive differs from a program reading an unlocked document. A protected key component does not make every application immune to attack.
questions.answer: File encryption protects selected files or folders. Full-disk or volume encryption protects stored contents against offline access when keys are unavailable. A self-encrypting drive performs encryption in its controller. A TPM (Trusted Platform Module) supports platform-bound key protection and measured-state uses; it is not simply a chip that encrypts all files or always refuses every altered boot. An HSM (Hardware Security Module) is a dedicated cryptographic key/operation boundary often serving applications or multiple systems. Hardware and firmware still require trustworthy implementation, configuration, and access controls. Recovery keys and backups are necessary operational considerations.
questions.example: A company may use disk encryption for lost laptops and an HSM (Hardware Security Module) for server signing keys. Neither prevents all misuse by an already authenticated running application.
questions.correct: File encryption protects selected files; disk encryption protects stored drive data; TPM and HSM protect particular keys and cryptographic operations.
distractors: A TPM automatically encrypts every network packet
Hardware encryption has no possible vulnerabilities
File encryption always protects every temporary file on the disk
questions.goal: Explain File encryption full-disk encryption and hardware in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A TPM automatically encrypts every network packet
questions.originalPrompt: How do file encryption, disk encryption, TPM, HSM, and self-encrypting drives differ?

setting.object: A laptop holds sensitive files, and some may be open in applications.
setting.location: Stored drive data, files in working memory, and key-protection components.
setting.purpose: Match protection to stored data, traveling data, or data currently being used.
setting.action: File or disk encryption protects selected stored contents. TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and HSM (Hardware Security Module) protect particular keys and operations. An unlocked application can still expose readable information.
setting.example: A company may use disk encryption for lost laptops and an HSM (Hardware Security Module) for server signing keys. Neither prevents all misuse by an already authenticated running application.

questions.title: Cryptography resource tradeoffs
questions.q: Why must a battery-powered device consider processing time, memory, energy, and response delay when using cryptography?
questions.teach: A small device may have little memory and battery power. A time-sensitive application also needs a timely response. Use appropriate secure designs and implementations rather than assuming stronger-looking settings have no resource cost.
questions.answer: Low-power sensors have limited energy and processing resources. Low-latency services must return results promptly. Lightweight cryptography aims to provide appropriate security within constrained environments; it is not permission to invent a weak cipher. Hardware acceleration can shift performance tradeoffs, but key management and implementation still matter. Evaluate the required property, threat, resource budget, and operational life rather than assuming the algorithm with the largest number is automatically the best system design.
questions.example: A battery-powered sensor needs authenticated readings without exhausting its battery. The design must protect integrity while meeting its power and timing budget.
questions.correct: Security operations consume limited resources, so the implementation must meet security requirements within the device’s operating limits.
distractors: Constrained devices need no authentication
Low latency means unlimited delay
Hardware acceleration removes all key-management risk
questions.goal: Explain Cryptography resource tradeoffs in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Constrained devices need no authentication
questions.originalPrompt: Why do low power and low latency affect cryptographic design?

setting.location: The implemented protocol, algorithm, software, and device resources.
setting.purpose: Provide appropriate security without ignoring implementation errors or operating limits.
setting.action: Weak algorithms, forced weaker settings, and programming mistakes create different problems. Resource limits affect implementation choices but do not justify assuming insecure choices are safe.
setting.example: A battery-powered sensor needs authenticated readings without exhausting its battery. The design must protect integrity while meeting its power and timing budget.

questions.title: Stuxnet and misleading visibility
questions.q: What does the lecture’s Stuxnet example teach about targeted systems and monitoring?
questions.teach: The lesson is the combination of several attack paths and misleading observations, not a list of old numerical claims.
questions.answer: Lecture 1 describes Stuxnet as a worm targeting industrial systems, using multiple previously unknown vulnerabilities and removable-media entry, and altering equipment behavior while showing apparently normal readings. Use it to explain targeted cyber-physical impact, trusted-looking telemetry, and the limits of perimeter isolation. The lecture’s dates and impact estimates are historical course claims. For an exam scenario, connect removable-media policy, endpoint controls, segmentation, independent monitoring, and recovery.
questions.example: An industrial operator sees normal readings while physical equipment behaves abnormally. Independent evidence is needed before treating one display as complete visibility.
questions.correct: Targeted malware can combine entry methods with deceptive monitoring
distractors: Air gaps make removable-media controls unnecessary
Every zero-day attack is Stuxnet
Normal displayed readings prove the machine is healthy
questions.goal: Explain Stuxnet and misleading visibility in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Air gaps make removable-media controls unnecessary

setting.object: Industrial equipment reports apparently normal readings while targeted malware interferes with operations.
setting.location: Control equipment, associated computers, and the monitoring information they provide.
setting.purpose: Recognize that compromised components can produce misleading observations.
setting.action: The Stuxnet example connects targeted compromise with deceptive monitoring. Independent evidence and appropriate system boundaries matter.
setting.example: An industrial operator sees normal readings while physical equipment behaves abnormally. Independent evidence is needed before treating one display as complete visibility.

questions.title: Choose the security device
questions.q: Which controls directly fit blocking an IP address, filtering website categories, and restricting unapproved programs?
questions.teach: An IP (Internet Protocol) rule evaluates traffic addresses. A web proxy handles web requests and applies site policies. Application allowlisting controls which software may run. Monitoring an event is different from blocking it.
questions.answer: Lecture 2’s cases select firewalls/router ACLs or prevention for malicious connection sources; a proxy is the strongest course answer for blocking website categories; application allowlisting restricts unapproved programs. A passive IDS (Intrusion Detection System) can alert but cannot itself guarantee a block. Host controls add visibility into local events. A packet sensor must actually receive the relevant traffic to observe it. Combine controls where the business case requires more than one kind of enforcement.
questions.example: A school needs to restrict gambling sites and stop unknown executables. A web proxy addresses the browsing policy; application controls address execution.
questions.correct: Firewall or ACL rules for an IP address; a filtering proxy for websites; application allowlisting for program execution.
distractors: A passive IDS alone guarantees all blocks
PCAP alone prevents execution
A checksum enforces website categories
questions.goal: Explain Choose the security device in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A passive IDS alone guarantees all blocks
questions.originalPrompt: Which control best fits an IP block, a website category policy, or unapproved execution?

setting.object: A company wants to deny an address, block website categories, and prevent unapproved programs from running.
setting.location: Network rules, application intermediaries, and endpoint execution policy.
setting.purpose: Choose enforcement at the place where the unwanted action happens.
setting.action: Firewall or ACL (Access Control List) rules can block traffic attributes; proxies can enforce application policies; application allowlisting restricts execution. Merely observing an event is not the same as preventing it.
setting.example: A school needs to restrict gambling sites and stop unknown executables. A web proxy addresses the browsing policy; application controls address execution.

questions.title: Detection tuning and business cost
questions.q: A legitimate nightly backup repeatedly causes attack alerts. How should the security team adjust detection?
questions.teach: Tune detection means adjust the rules using investigated evidence. First confirm why the backup triggered the alert. Then reduce that harmless alert without disabling useful attack detection. Consider business impact: needless blocking interrupts work, but hiding genuine attacks leaves the organization exposed.
questions.answer: A detection signature may be a byte pattern, behavior rule, hash, or other feature; it is not always one unique hexadecimal string embedded in the file. Anomaly detection may notice new behavior but can flag unusual legitimate work. A false positive can overload analysts or interrupt service when prevention acts; a false negative can let an attack continue. Tuning uses representative traffic and investigation feedback. Redundancy, scalability, and business needs constrain inspection design.
questions.example: A large legitimate backup suddenly triggers an anomaly rule. The team investigates and adjusts the rule without disabling monitoring for all other traffic.
questions.correct: Investigate the backup, adjust the relevant rule carefully, and verify that actual attacks still generate alerts.
distractors: Every anomaly is malicious
Every signature is guaranteed unique
A zero alert rate proves perfect security
questions.goal: Explain Detection tuning and business cost in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every anomaly is malicious
questions.originalPrompt: How do signature detection, anomaly detection, and tuning affect decisions?

setting.object: A monitoring system warns about a network transfer that may be an attack or a legitimate backup.
setting.location: The security alert and the network or host activity that triggered it.
setting.purpose: Decide whether the alert represents a real problem and choose an appropriate response.
setting.action: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) alerts; IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can intervene. Investigated evidence helps tune rules without hiding real attacks or unnecessarily blocking normal work.
setting.example: A large legitimate backup suddenly triggers an anomaly rule. The team investigates and adjusts the rule without disabling monitoring for all other traffic.

questions.title: Defacement and advance-fee scams
questions.q: How do changing a website and a 419 scam differ in mechanism and business harm?
questions.teach: Defacement changes what a site displays. An advance-fee scam persuades a person to give money or information for a promised reward.
questions.answer: A site defacement may exploit a software weakness or stolen administrative credentials to alter public content, creating reputational and integrity harm. Defenses include safe configuration, updates, strong access control, restricted publishing privileges, monitoring, and restoration. A 419 scam builds trust around a claimed inheritance, lottery, or similar payout and then requests fees or sensitive information. Use independent verification and approved reporting, not participation in the claimed transaction.
questions.example: A changed homepage announcing false claims is a defacement. A message offering a large reward if an employee first pays a handling fee is advance-fee fraud.
questions.correct: Defacement attacks content integrity; advance-fee fraud manipulates trust
distractors: Both necessarily use the same database exploit
419 is a cryptographic hash
A defacement is always a harmless prank
questions.goal: Explain Defacement and advance-fee scams in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Both necessarily use the same database exploit

setting.object: A person receives a convincing message promising a reward, or a website’s visible page is changed without permission.
setting.location: Email, text messages, calls, payment requests, or published website content.
setting.purpose: Distinguish manipulation of people from unauthorized changes to website content.
setting.action: Social-engineering categories depend on targeting and delivery channel. Advance-fee fraud asks for payment first; defacement changes the visible site.
setting.example: A changed homepage announcing false claims is a defacement. A message offering a large reward if an employee first pays a handling fee is advance-fee fraud.

questions.title: Investigating an email without trusting it
