questions.q: What evidence should you compare when reviewing a suspicious message?
questions.teach: Separate the message’s claims from evidence added by trusted receiving systems. A name, logo, or urgent story is easy to imitate.
questions.answer: Review sender/display name, sending domain, reply and return paths, routing hops, time/time zones, recipients, subject, and attachment/link context. Authentication results from a trusted receiver provide useful evidence but need interpretation. A mismatch or failed check can be significant; a pass does not prove the message’s business request is safe. Use known contact details to verify unusual requests. Preserve/report the original message according to the organization’s process.
questions.example: A message names a real professor but asks students to sign in on a lookalike site. The familiar name does not establish that the link or request is legitimate.
questions.correct: Compare trusted header evidence with claimed identity and request context
distractors: A university logo proves identity
A display name proves the domain
A clean-looking body replaces header review
questions.goal: Explain Investigating an email without trusting it in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A university logo proves identity

setting.object: An email claims the recipient must urgently reset a university password.
setting.location: The received message, full headers, links, and mail-system records.
setting.purpose: Investigate the claimed sender and request without trusting the display name.
setting.action: Compare routing and authentication evidence, sender domains, timing, and the request with a trusted reporting or verification process.
setting.example: A message names a real professor but asks students to sign in on a lookalike site. The familiar name does not establish that the link or request is legitimate.

questions.title: Fake antivirus and fake disk repair
questions.q: Why do professional-looking warnings still need independent verification?
questions.teach: Scareware sells fear. A convincing screen can invent an infection or disk failure to pressure installation or payment.
questions.answer: Lecture 4 distinguishes fake antivirus/rogueware and fake disk-defragmenter products. Both invent problems and request money or installation; installed malware may interfere with real security software or capture data. A polished interface and large scan count are claims, not proof. Use trusted support and already-approved security tools. If someone installed the product, investigate the endpoint and account activity rather than merely closing the warning.
questions.example: A website reports hundreds of disk errors and demands a fee. A page cannot establish that claim simply by displaying a scan animation.
questions.correct: Verify warnings using trusted tools and support before acting
distractors: A professional icon proves the product is legitimate
Every browser warning means the disk was scanned
Paying always removes the infection
questions.goal: Explain Fake antivirus and fake disk repair in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A professional icon proves the product is legitimate

setting.object: A pop-up claims the computer is infected or the drive is failing and demands payment or installation.
setting.location: An employee’s screen and the source of the warning.
setting.purpose: Verify the claim without following an attacker’s instructions.
setting.action: Use known trusted security tools and support channels. A professional appearance and urgent wording do not establish that a warning is legitimate.
setting.example: A website reports hundreds of disk errors and demands a fee. A page cannot establish that claim simply by displaying a scan animation.

questions.title: Controlled hardening and patch validation
questions.q: Why test small groups of hardening changes and verify the rollout?
questions.teach: A control must improve security while preserving required work. Small, measured changes are easier to troubleshoot than a hundred unexplained changes.
questions.answer: Apply an appropriate baseline, test representative systems, stage changes, schedule deployment where necessary, and verify success with rollback available. Remove unnecessary services and limit privileged access. A firewall can reduce exposure to a vulnerable service, but that does not repair the flaw or eliminate other attack paths. Legacy tools such as EMET, WSUS, or old scanner screenshots illustrate functions, not a requirement to install historical versions. The four discussion factors reduce distribution, coordination, analysis, and testing pressure.
questions.example: Five baseline changes are tested before rollout. A broken business application can then be traced to a small set of candidate changes.
questions.correct: Test staged changes and confirm both security and required functionality
distractors: Apply every change without records
Blocked traffic proves all flaws are fixed
Snapshots guarantee no future outage
questions.goal: Explain Controlled hardening and patch validation in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Apply every change without records

setting.object: An IT (Information Technology) team must install security updates on many company computers without breaking work.
setting.location: Update distribution, test devices, deployment records, and production systems.
setting.purpose: Repair weaknesses efficiently while verifying that needed services still work.
setting.action: Bandwidth helps distribute updates; centralized services coordinate; analytics prioritizes; virtual machines support testing. Stage changes and verify the results.
setting.example: Five baseline changes are tested before rollout. A broken business application can then be traced to a small set of candidate changes.

questions.title: NAC policy and endpoint controls
questions.q: How do NAC, GPO, endpoint firewall, and HIPS contribute different protections?
questions.teach: NAC (Network Access Control) decides whether a device meets conditions for access. GPO (Group Policy Object) distributes settings. Endpoint firewall and HIPS (Host Intrusion Prevention System) enforce or observe activity on a host.
questions.answer: Lecture 5 uses a traveling workstation to explain posture checks: patch status, antivirus definitions, and required policies can influence access. GPO (Group Policy Object) helps distribute Windows-domain policy settings. An endpoint firewall restricts network communication to host services, while HIPS (Host Intrusion Prevention System) can respond to selected local behaviors or patterns. None eliminates the need to verify actual configuration, investigate alerts, or protect accounts. A domain user can still have excessive rights if configured incorrectly.
questions.example: A returning laptop is checked before receiving normal access. Its required firewall policy must also be present and effective after connection.
questions.correct: Access posture, configuration distribution, and local enforcement complement each other
distractors: GPO automatically authenticates every external site
A domain account can never be privileged
NAC replaces all patch deployment
questions.goal: Explain NAC (Network Access Control) policy and endpoint controls in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: GPO automatically authenticates every external site

setting.object: An administrator configures a staff laptop before allowing normal work and network access.
setting.location: The device’s accounts, operating-system settings, services, updates, and local security controls.
setting.purpose: Reduce unnecessary exposure and enforce appropriate access and execution rules.
setting.action: Use standard accounts, patch software, disable unneeded services, configure host protections, and verify required settings. NAC (Network Access Control), GPO (Group Policy Object), endpoint firewalls, and HIPS (Host Intrusion Prevention System) perform different jobs.
setting.example: A returning laptop is checked before receiving normal access. Its required firewall policy must also be present and effective after connection.

questions.title: Manual automated static and dynamic
questions.q: How do manual analysis, automated analysis, static analysis, and dynamic analysis differ?
questions.teach: These are the four labels. Manual versus automated describes who performs the analysis. Static versus dynamic describes whether the program being examined runs. A person can read code manually and statically; a tool can automatically observe it running dynamically.
questions.answer: A person can read source statically or debug running code dynamically. A tool can automate either approach. Lecture 6 names Firebug and Malzilla for manual review and JSUnpack, Wepawet, and reputation services under automated tools. Inspect source for suspicious redirects, embedded frames, scripts, form handling, and external references. Legitimate pages can contain those features too, so context and behavior matter. JSUnpack is the sample answer. It unpacks JavaScript and can emulate execution; automated tools can combine static and dynamic techniques.
questions.example: A script automatically scans source without executing it: automated/static. A human watches an isolated program’s network changes: manual/dynamic.
questions.correct: Manual means a person does the work; automated means software does it; static avoids execution; dynamic observes execution.
distractors: All automated analysis is static
All manual analysis executes code
Every iframe proves malware
questions.goal: Explain Manual automated static and dynamic in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: All automated analysis is static
questions.originalPrompt: Why are these four analysis labels not interchangeable?

setting.object: An analyst examines a suspicious web page and its scripts.
setting.location: Page source, an isolated test browser, and website-analysis services.
setting.purpose: Determine what the page does and interpret the evidence behind a safety rating.
setting.action: Static analysis inspects without executing; dynamic analysis observes execution. Manual and automated describe who performs the work; reputation summarizes observations.
setting.example: A script automatically scans source without executing it: automated/static. A human watches an isolated program’s network changes: manual/dynamic.

questions.title: Reputation and behavior evidence
questions.q: Why can a website’s reputation label disagree with a new behavior test?
questions.teach: A reputation label is a service’s rating of a site based on observations such as previous scans. It is not a permanent safety guarantee. Compare when the tests ran, what each observed, and whether each reached the same content.
questions.answer: Reputation services rely on their scan history, reporting, and classification. A newly compromised legitimate page may not yet be listed. Different user agents, times, or visitor conditions may receive different content. Dynamic inspection observes files, registry, processes, and connections in a controlled environment; a negative result may reflect the test conditions. Isolation reduces risk but is not an absolute guarantee. Do not browse historical malicious domains from lecture screenshots as study exercises.
questions.example: One service reports an old clean scan, while a sandbox sees a new redirect only for a particular browser. The evidence needs reconciliation, not blind voting.
questions.correct: A reputation rating reflects earlier observations; the website or the conditions of the new test may have changed.
distractors: A recognizable URL guarantees safety forever
One clean reputation score proves no compromise
A VM can never affect its host
questions.goal: Explain Reputation and behavior evidence in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A recognizable URL guarantees safety forever
questions.originalPrompt: Why can two website scanners disagree, and why does time matter?

setting.object: An analyst examines a suspicious web page and its scripts.
setting.location: Page source, an isolated test browser, and website-analysis services.
setting.purpose: Determine what the page does and interpret the evidence behind a safety rating.
setting.action: Static analysis inspects without executing; dynamic analysis observes execution. Manual and automated describe who performs the work; reputation summarizes observations.
setting.example: One service reports an old clean scan, while a sandbox sees a new redirect only for a particular browser. The evidence needs reconciliation, not blind voting.

questions.title: Merkle proofs and hash links
questions.q: How does a Merkle proof differ from a link to the previous block?
questions.teach: One commitment summarizes transactions inside a block. Another connects that block to earlier history.
questions.answer: A Merkle tree combines transaction hashes into a root. A membership proof supplies enough sibling hashes to recompute the trusted root without downloading every transaction. It shows inclusion under that root, not that a real-world claim is true or a spend valid. A previous-block hash commits to the preceding header. Non-membership proofs require appropriate ordered/authenticated structures; not every ordinary Merkle tree automatically proves absence. Changing data affects its commitment and descendant links.
questions.example: A lightweight client can verify inclusion using a transaction and its proof path, but still needs an appropriately trusted chain/header view and validation assumptions.
questions.correct: Merkle proofs show inclusion under a root; prior hashes link block history
distractors: A Merkle proof reveals every owner’s private key
Membership proves every business claim is true
Any unsorted tree automatically proves absence
questions.goal: Explain Merkle proofs and hash links in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A Merkle proof reveals every owner’s private key

setting.object: A block records transactions and points to earlier blockchain history.
setting.location: Transaction hashes, the Merkle tree, block-header fields, and the previous-block hash.
setting.purpose: Summarize included transactions and make changes to linked history detectable.
setting.action: A Merkle root commits to transactions; a proof checks inclusion under that root. The previous-block hash links history; a proof-of-work nonce is varied during the mining search.
setting.example: A lightweight client can verify inclusion using a transaction and its proof path, but still needs an appropriately trusted chain/header view and validation assumptions.

questions.title: Consensus double spending and forks
questions.q: Why can two validly signed Bitcoin transactions still conflict by trying to spend the same funds?
questions.teach: Double spending means trying to use the same digital funds twice. A person controlling a key can sign two conflicting transactions. A valid signature shows authorization, not that the funds remain unspent. Nodes check unspent outputs and agree on a valid history.
questions.answer: Nodes independently validate transactions and blocks. Bitcoin’s proof-of-work chain selection follows greatest cumulative work among valid chains; the lecture’s longest-chain phrase is a simplification. The Byzantine-generals theme concerns agreement despite faulty or malicious participants. Confirmations reduce reorganization risk under the security assumptions. A hard fork changes rules incompatibly; a soft fork restricts accepted rules compatibly for older nodes. Neither term simply means every competing branch survives or disappears by natural selection.
questions.example: Two transactions spend the same previous output and both have genuine owner signatures. They cannot both enter the same valid transaction history.
questions.correct: A signature authorizes a spend; validation and consensus must also prevent the same output from being spent twice.
distractors: A valid signature makes every conflicting spend acceptable
Any chain with more block count is always valid
Every hard fork guarantees two permanent chains
refs: security challenges chain selection and forks
questions.goal: Explain Consensus double spending and forks in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A valid signature makes every conflicting spend acceptable
questions.originalPrompt: Why do valid signatures alone not solve the double-spending problem?

setting.object: Two groups follow different rules for accepting blockchain records, or two payments try to spend the same funds.
setting.location: The transaction ledger maintained by participating computers.
setting.purpose: Understand agreement about which valid transaction history is accepted.
setting.action: Validation and consensus resolve competing histories. Incompatible rule changes can produce a hard fork when participants continue separate histories.
setting.example: Two transactions spend the same previous output and both have genuine owner signatures. They cannot both enter the same valid transaction history.

questions.title: Packets encapsulation and headers
questions.q: What is the usual nesting of an application message inside TCP/IP communication?
questions.teach: Each layer adds its own control information. The IP (Internet Protocol) payload can include a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) header and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) data. The frame carries the IP (Internet Protocol) packet across a particular local link.
questions.answer: Application data can be carried in a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segment with ports, sequence/acknowledgment fields, and a checksum. IP (Internet Protocol) wraps transport data with addresses and routing-related header fields. A link-layer frame carries the IP (Internet Protocol) packet on a particular link. Packet lengths vary within protocol/link constraints. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is transport/OSI layer 4; IP (Internet Protocol) is network/OSI layer 3. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does not choose the Internet route or provide encryption. Checksum error detection is distinct from authenticated integrity.
questions.example: A short message gains TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) headers before link transmission. A capture can show ports and addresses even when higher-level contents are encrypted.
questions.correct: Application data is carried in a TCP segment, which is carried in an IP packet, which is carried in a link-layer frame.
distractors: TCP contains the entire Internet routing table
Every IP packet has the same fixed size
IP automatically encrypts the payload
questions.goal: Explain Packets encapsulation and headers in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: TCP contains the entire Internet routing table
questions.originalPrompt: How do application data, TCP segments, and IP packets fit together?

setting.object: A laptop sends file data to a server across a network.
setting.location: The application, transport service, IP (Internet Protocol) network, and local links.
setting.purpose: Understand which layer handles reliable delivery, separate messages, and forwarding.
setting.action: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides separate datagrams without those guarantees; IP (Internet Protocol) forwards packets toward destinations.
setting.example: A short message gains TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) headers before link transmission. A capture can show ports and addresses even when higher-level contents are encrypted.

questions.title: Firewall types and return-traffic assumptions
questions.q: How do packet-filtering firewalls, connection-aware controls, and application gateways inspect different information?
questions.teach: Different controls can see and enforce different things. Allowing a port does not prove the carried activity is safe. Proxy inspection and connection tracking also depend on their configured rules and visibility.
questions.answer: The lecture diagram associates packet filtering with network-level checks, circuit gateways with connection/session establishment, application gateways with higher-level mediation, and MAC-layer controls with link identifiers. Modern products may combine capabilities. Stateful filtering tracks connection context; a simplistic rule allowing anything resembling return traffic can be misleading. A proxy may authenticate users and restrict requests, but its visibility and policies determine effectiveness. Compare business goals and inspectable evidence rather than assuming one name guarantees protection.
questions.example: A network rule sees an IP (Internet Protocol) and port; an application proxy can apply a website-category policy. Neither replaces endpoint evidence about which process initiated a connection.
questions.correct: Packet filters inspect fields such as addresses and ports; connection-aware controls consider connection context; application gateways can apply application-specific rules.
distractors: Every allowed ACK proves an established session
A proxy always defeats every reverse shell
MAC filtering verifies a person’s identity
questions.goal: Explain Firewall types and return-traffic assumptions in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every allowed ACK proves an established session
questions.originalPrompt: How do packet filtering, circuit gateways, and application gateways differ?

setting.object: A company wants to deny an address, block website categories, and prevent unapproved programs from running.
setting.location: Network rules, application intermediaries, and endpoint execution policy.
setting.purpose: Choose enforcement at the place where the unwanted action happens.
setting.action: Firewall or ACL (Access Control List) rules can block traffic attributes; proxies can enforce application policies; application allowlisting restricts execution. Merely observing an event is not the same as preventing it.
setting.example: A network rule sees an IP (Internet Protocol) and port; an application proxy can apply a website-category policy. Neither replaces endpoint evidence about which process initiated a connection.

questions.title: Secure protocol choices
questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes FTPS, SFTP, HTTPS, S/MIME, SRTP, and NTP?
questions.teach: Start with the application task, then identify its protection. FTPS (File Transfer Protocol over Transport Layer Security) and SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) use different protocols. Ordinary NTP (Network Time Protocol) does not automatically provide cryptographic protection. A secure-looking name is not a substitute for checking how the service is actually configured.
questions.answer: Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) uses separate control/data connections without encryption. FTPS (File Transfer Protocol over Transport Layer Security) adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) to FTP (File Transfer Protocol); require the intended protection for control and data rather than assuming both are protected. SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) is file transfer over SSH (Secure Shell), not FTP (File Transfer Protocol) with a secure label. HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) protects HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) with TLS (Transport Layer Security). S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) supports email content signing/encryption, subject to key and client support. SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) protects real-time media. NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronizes time; plain NTP (Network Time Protocol) alone is not a cryptographic guarantee (NTS (Network Time Security) is a separate security mechanism). DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) authenticates DNS (Domain Name System) data and does not encrypt ordinary queries. These clarify the lecture’s simplified secure-protocol table.
questions.example: A company moving files chooses SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) over SSH (Secure Shell). A signed email may remain signed beyond one transport connection, unlike merely protecting its delivery link with TLS (Transport Layer Security).
questions.correct: FTPS protects FTP with TLS; SFTP transfers files over SSH; HTTPS protects web traffic; S/MIME protects email content; SRTP protects media; NTP synchronizes clocks.
distractors: SFTP and FTPS are identical
Plain NTP guarantees authenticated time
DNSSEC encrypts every web connection
refs: secure file transfer email and protocol table
questions.goal: Explain Secure protocol choices in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: SFTP and FTPS are identical
questions.originalPrompt: How do FTP, FTPS, SFTP, HTTPS, S/MIME, SRTP, and NTP differ?

setting.object: An administrator selects services for web access, file transfer, email, device management, and clock synchronization.
setting.location: Clients, servers, protocol configuration, and communication paths.
setting.purpose: Choose the correct service and verify what protection is actually provided.
setting.action: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), FTPS (File Transfer Protocol over Transport Layer Security), SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol), S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), and SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) protect different applications. DNS (Domain Name System), SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), and NTP (Network Time Protocol) have distinct jobs; their ordinary names do not guarantee every security property.
setting.example: A company moving files chooses SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol) over SSH (Secure Shell). A signed email may remain signed beyond one transport connection, unlike merely protecting its delivery link with TLS (Transport Layer Security).

questions.title: DNS SNMP and diagnostic evidence
questions.q: What distinct information do DNS, SNMP, and ICMP provide to a network administrator?
questions.teach: A DNS (Domain Name System) lookup investigates name resolution. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) can report managed device status. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) messages help diagnose reachability or delivery problems. Each gives only part of the evidence; none proves every application is working correctly.
questions.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) provides hierarchical distributed name records. Poisoning can redirect resolution; validated DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) checks signed DNS (Domain Name System) data. Restricting unintended zone transfer reduces information exposure. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) agents expose permitted management information; versions 1/2c use community strings, while v3 supports stronger authentication/privacy depending on configuration. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo can test reachability and latency, but a blocked response does not prove the host is down. A successful ping does not prove that an application works.
questions.example: A device answers ping but its web application fails. The network evidence establishes only part of the service path, so application logs and connection tests are needed.
questions.correct: DNS provides name records; SNMP provides device-management information; ICMP provides network-control and diagnostic messages.
distractors: A successful ping proves every application is healthy
SNMP community strings always encrypt traffic
DNSSEC makes all returned websites trustworthy
questions.goal: Explain DNS (Domain Name System) SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) and diagnostic evidence in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A successful ping proves every application is healthy
questions.originalPrompt: What can DNS, SNMP, and ICMP tell an administrator?

setting.object: An administrator selects services for web access, file transfer, email, device management, and clock synchronization.
setting.location: Clients, servers, protocol configuration, and communication paths.
setting.purpose: Choose the correct service and verify what protection is actually provided.
setting.action: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), FTPS (File Transfer Protocol over Transport Layer Security), SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol), S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), and SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) protect different applications. DNS (Domain Name System), SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), and NTP (Network Time Protocol) have distinct jobs; their ordinary names do not guarantee every security property.
setting.example: A device answers ping but its web application fails. The network evidence establishes only part of the service path, so application logs and connection tests are needed.

questions.title: Port mirrors taps and sensor placement
questions.q: Why might a network sensor miss an attack occurring elsewhere in the organization?
questions.teach: A switch mirror copies selected traffic and a tap observes a link. Neither automatically sees every device everywhere. Combine network observations with endpoint and account records where necessary.
questions.answer: A switch mirror copies selected port traffic to a monitoring port. A network tap provides a traffic copy from a link. Both have operational limitations; traffic may be dropped, selected incompletely, or remain encrypted. Sensors detect, collectors gather, filters enforce, and correlation engines combine evidence. Placement should cover relevant boundaries, internal movement, and business assets; simply choosing the busiest link can miss a smaller critical segment. TLS (Transport Layer Security) termination changes which content may be visible.
questions.example: A gateway sensor sees Internet traffic but not two servers talking locally on another switch. An internal mirror or other telemetry may be needed.
questions.correct: The sensor sees only traffic that actually reaches its monitored link or copied traffic feed.
distractors: The busiest link reveals every network action
Mirroring automatically decrypts TLS
A collector always blocks malware inline
questions.goal: Explain Port mirrors taps and sensor placement in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: The busiest link reveals every network action
questions.originalPrompt: Why does sensor placement determine what defenders can see?

setting.object: An analyst needs evidence about traffic leaving a company laptop.
setting.location: A monitored network link, packet captures, connection summaries, and proxy records.
setting.purpose: Choose evidence that can answer who communicated, when, how much, and potentially what was carried.
setting.action: PCAP (Packet Capture) records observed packet bytes; flow records summarize connections. Mirrors and taps determine what the sensor can see. A proxy handles requests; allowlisting controls software execution.
setting.example: A gateway sensor sees Internet traffic but not two servers talking locally on another switch. An internal mirror or other telemetry may be needed.

questions.title: Logs correlation and retention
questions.q: How should an investigator use login, process, network, and file logs together?
questions.teach: Each record shows only part of the story. Matching related records helps identify what happened and which systems are affected. Missing logs or inconsistent clocks limit the conclusions.
questions.answer: Access logs show resource requests, audit logs record accountable actions, event logs record system/application events, and security logs describe security-related observations. Exact fields vary. Correlate identity, host, and network events using reliable time and context. Watch rejected traffic, unusual outbound connections, unsuccessful logins, and unexpected file changes. Centralized analysis helps handle volume and format differences, but collection gaps, clock differences, retention limits, and tampering affect conclusions. File-integrity monitoring detects changes; an alert still needs interpretation.
questions.example: An unusual login precedes a new process and outbound transfer. Together these support a stronger timeline than any one record alone.
questions.correct: Compare their times and event details to reconstruct activity, while checking missing records, clock differences, and how long evidence was kept.
distractors: One log contains every action forever
No retained event proves nothing happened
All file changes are definitely malicious
refs: analyzing security data and log management
questions.goal: Explain Logs correlation and retention in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: One log contains every action forever
questions.originalPrompt: How do access audit event and security logs support an investigation?

setting.object: A staff login is followed by an unusual program launch and an outbound transfer.
setting.location: Account logs, endpoint process and file events, and network records.
setting.purpose: Reconstruct related events, assess affected systems, and decide containment actions.
setting.action: Correlate timestamps and details rather than assuming one alert proves all data was stolen. Check clock accuracy, record coverage, and how long logs were retained.
setting.example: An unusual login precedes a new process and outbound transfer. Together these support a stronger timeline than any one record alone.

questions.title: Hypervisors containers and virtual desktops
questions.q: How do Type I hypervisors, Type II hypervisors, containers, and VDI differ?
questions.teach: A hypervisor manages virtual machines. A container usually shares the host kernel rather than having the same boundary as a complete guest OS (Operating System). VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) describes delivery of desktops. VM (Virtual Machine) sprawl means uncontrolled growth that makes inventory and patching difficult.
questions.answer: Type I hypervisors run directly on hardware; Type II hypervisors run above a host OS (Operating System), as in the VirtualBox lab. Containers package applications and dependencies while sharing a kernel, with different isolation boundaries from VMs. VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) hosts user desktops on servers. Snapshots and live migration support operations but do not automatically remove downtime or replace backups. VM (Virtual Machine) escape is a possible isolation failure; VM (Virtual Machine) sprawl is unmanaged growth. Protect the hypervisor, guests, management plane, and virtual networks. Virtual Distributed Ethernet (VDE) describes a virtual Ethernet network connecting virtual and/or physical systems; it is a networking concept, distinct from VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure)’s remotely hosted desktops.
questions.example: An organization creates twenty test VMs and forgets half of them. Those systems still need ownership, updates, and monitoring.
questions.correct: Type I runs on hardware; Type II runs on a host OS; containers commonly share a kernel; VDI provides remotely accessed desktops.
distractors: Every container has its own full guest kernel
A snapshot is an independent backup by definition
VMs never need security updates
questions.goal: Explain Hypervisors containers and virtual desktops in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every container has its own full guest kernel
questions.originalPrompt: How do Type I Type II containers VDI and VM sprawl differ?

setting.object: A student runs intentionally vulnerable guest machines for a controlled lab.
setting.location: Virtualization software, guest operating systems, virtual network adapters, and saved states.
setting.purpose: Keep experiments controlled and distinguish the guest environment from the physical host.
setting.action: Hypervisors manage guests; network settings affect reachability; snapshots help restore states. Containers, VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure), and uncontrolled VM (Virtual Machine) growth have different boundaries and management concerns.
setting.example: An organization creates twenty test VMs and forgets half of them. Those systems still need ownership, updates, and monitoring.

questions.title: Cloud models and responsibility
questions.q: How do SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS change what the customer manages?
questions.teach: The service arrangement determines which duties belong to the provider or customer. Accounts, data, access choices, and configuration still require attention. Public, private, community, and hybrid describe deployment arrangements rather than these service layers.
questions.answer: SaaS (Software as a Service) supplies an application; PaaS (Platform as a Service) supplies a managed platform for customer applications; IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) supplies infrastructure where customers manage their OS (Operating System)/applications. SECaaS delivers security services. Public/private/community/hybrid describe deployment arrangements, not the same categories as service models. Protect identities, configurations, data, transmission, tenant isolation, and availability according to responsibility. A CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) helps extend enterprise policy to cloud usage. Distributed processing does not by itself mean every participant has equal authority. A public cloud offers provider services to customers generally; a private cloud is dedicated to one organization; a community cloud serves organizations with shared needs; a hybrid combines distinct cloud arrangements with integration. These describe deployment, while SaaS (Software as a Service)/PaaS (Platform as a Service)/IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) describe which service layers are supplied.
questions.example: An IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) customer still patches its own guest OS (Operating System). A SaaS (Software as a Service) customer may not patch the vendor’s servers but still controls its own user access and data-sharing choices.
questions.correct: SaaS supplies an application; PaaS supplies an application platform; IaaS supplies infrastructure while the customer manages guest operating systems and applications.
distractors: Cloud always means the provider patches every customer OS
Private cloud means there is no network
SaaS and hybrid are the same kind of category
questions.goal: Explain Cloud models and responsibility in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Cloud always means the provider patches every customer OS
questions.originalPrompt: How do SaaS PaaS IaaS and cloud deployment models affect security duties?

setting.object: A business uses a provider’s hosted application, platform, or virtual server.
setting.location: The provider’s infrastructure and the customer’s applications, accounts, data, and configuration.
setting.purpose: Determine which security work belongs to the provider and which still belongs to the customer.
setting.action: SaaS (Software as a Service) supplies an application; PaaS (Platform as a Service) supplies a platform; IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) supplies infrastructure. Responsibilities depend on the service arrangement and do not disappear when moving to the cloud.
setting.example: An IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) customer still patches its own guest OS (Operating System). A SaaS (Software as a Service) customer may not patch the vendor’s servers but still controls its own user access and data-sharing choices.

checks.q: A payroll file is encrypted before transfer. Someone who intercepts the file sees ciphertext and needs the appropriate decryption key to read it. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: True
distractors: False
checks.teach: Plaintext is the readable message. Ciphertext is its encrypted representation. A digest is a different kind of output.
checks.answer: TRUE. Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. Decryption recovers plaintext using the appropriate key. Hashing instead produces a digest for comparison and has no decryption operation.
checks.example: A payroll file is encrypted before transfer. Someone who intercepts the file sees ciphertext and needs the appropriate decryption key to read it.

setting.object: A private report stored as an encrypted file.
setting.location: A laptop’s storage drive and the application opening the file.
setting.purpose: Let authorized people recover the report while protecting it from unauthorized reading.
setting.action: Encryption transforms the contents into ciphertext; the appropriate decryption procedure and key recover plaintext.
setting.example: A payroll file is encrypted before transfer. Someone who intercepts the file sees ciphertext and needs the appropriate decryption key to read it.

checks.q: An attacker steals a student’s login and recovery information, then uses the account to impersonate the student or access additional services. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: True
distractors: False
checks.teach: Data can have value because it helps impersonate a person or reach another account. Payment details are only one target.
checks.answer: TRUE. Personal information, credentials, health records, private communications, and intellectual property can support fraud, extortion, resale, and espionage. The textbook’s social-engineering example shows why account-recovery information can be valuable even without a full card number.
checks.example: An attacker steals a student’s login and recovery information, then uses the account to impersonate the student or access additional services.

setting.object: A stolen student login, address, and medical information.
setting.location: Account records and private files accessed through a compromised account.
setting.purpose: Understand why personal information is valuable even without payment-card details.
setting.action: An attacker may use stolen information for impersonation, fraud, resale, or extortion.
setting.example: An attacker steals a student’s login and recovery information, then uses the account to impersonate the student or access additional services.

checks.q: A fully patched employee enters a password on a cloned login page. The password is disclosed without exploiting a software flaw. Login monitoring and phishing-resistant MFA reduce the resulting risk. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: True
distractors: False because SET cannot collect credentials
True because SET always bypasses every control
False because SET is an encryption algorithm
checks.teach: A user trusts a deceptive page and submits credentials. A familiar appearance and a redirect to the real site can make the credential theft less noticeable.
checks.answer: TRUE. SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) means Social-Engineer Toolkit. Your SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) lab shows that a convincing fake login page can capture credentials through user interaction, and a redirect can conceal the deception. The key concept is social engineering: deception persuades the user to disclose information, reducing the attacker’s dependence on exploiting a software vulnerability.
checks.example: A fully patched employee enters a password on a cloned login page. The password is disclosed without exploiting a software flaw. Login monitoring and phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) reduce the resulting risk.

setting.object: A staff member enters a test password into a cloned login page.
setting.location: The employee’s browser and a credential-collection page in the authorized lab.
setting.purpose: Understand how a convincing page can obtain credentials through user interaction.
setting.action: The form submits the entered information to the collecting system. This alone does not prove malicious code ran on the employee’s computer.
setting.example: A fully patched employee enters a password on a cloned login page. The password is disclosed without exploiting a software flaw. Login monitoring and phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) reduce the resulting risk.

checks.q: A workstation makes an unusual outbound connection after a malicious process starts. Correlate process and network logs, isolate the host, and restrict unnecessary egress rather than relying solely on inbound rules. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: False: firewall effectiveness depends on its rules and inspection
distractors: Always true for every proxy
False because reverse shells only start inbound connections
True because a proxy encrypts every endpoint process
checks.teach: Direction and policy explain the result. Outbound does not mean automatically allowed, and proxy does not mean automatically secure.
checks.answer: FALSE as written. A reverse shell starts an outbound connection from a compromised internal host to an attacker. It can pass packet filters that allow that outbound traffic. A proxy can require authentication, restrict destinations and protocols, and inspect traffic, but its effectiveness depends on configuration and visibility. A properly configured proxy can block a raw shell connection by enforcing application protocols. A shell tunneled through an allowed application protocol still requires inspection and policy enforcement; the word proxy alone does not guarantee prevention.
checks.example: A workstation makes an unusual outbound connection after a malicious process starts. Correlate process and network logs, isolate the host, and restrict unnecessary egress rather than relying solely on inbound rules.

setting.object: A compromised workstation starts a command connection to an outside controller.
setting.location: A program on the workstation and its outbound network connection.
setting.purpose: Understand remote command access and why outbound traffic needs appropriate controls.
setting.action: A reverse shell starts its connection from the affected computer. Filtering depends on rules, protocol handling, and visibility.
setting.example: A workstation makes an unusual outbound connection after a malicious process starts. Correlate process and network logs, isolate the host, and restrict unnecessary egress rather than relying solely on inbound rules.

checks.q: A mail application resolves a server name with DNS, connects using transport protocols, and uses SMTP to send mail. Several suite members cooperate. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: True
distractors: False
checks.teach: The suite is the whole family. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) are central members with different jobs.
checks.answer: TRUE with a spelling correction: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), not SMPT. TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) names a protocol suite spanning layers. DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) supports device management, SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail, POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves mail, and FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transfers files. They are not all transport-layer protocols.
checks.example: A mail application resolves a server name with DNS (Domain Name System), connects using transport protocols, and uses SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) to send mail. Several suite members cooperate.

setting.object: A computer looks up a mail server, sends a message, and retrieves mail.
setting.location: The client, DNS (Domain Name System) service, mail servers, and network connections.
setting.purpose: Distinguish the communication jobs performed by different protocols.
setting.action: DNS (Domain Name System) looks up names; SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail; POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves mail. TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) is a family of cooperating protocols.
setting.example: A mail application resolves a server name with DNS (Domain Name System), connects using transport protocols, and uses SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) to send mail. Several suite members cooperate.

checks.q: An employee evaluates staff security needs and designs a suitable access-control solution while managing daily security technology. That matches the administrator role in the book. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Security administrator
distractors: Security technician
Security officer
Security manager
checks.teach: Match the duties to this textbook’s definition. Job titles at actual companies can vary.
checks.answer: A. Security administrator. Ciampa Chapter 1, printed page 6 (PDF page 34), assigns these duties to the security administrator. A technician configures and troubleshoots tools; a manager supervises personnel; the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) directs security at the executive level. This resolves the second guide’s textbook-needed placeholder.
checks.example: An employee evaluates staff security needs and designs a suitable access-control solution while managing daily security technology. That matches the administrator role in the book.

setting.object: An organization hires staff to design security, configure tools, and supervise the team.
setting.location: The organization’s security department and its supported systems.
setting.purpose: Match a job’s actual duties to the textbook’s role definitions.
setting.action: The administrator designs solutions for users, the technician configures and troubleshoots tools, and the manager supervises personnel.
setting.example: An employee evaluates staff security needs and designs a suitable access-control solution while managing daily security technology. That matches the administrator role in the book.

checks.q: Two checkout requests both see one remaining item before either updates stock. Both complete, selling the same item twice. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Concurrent execution accesses a shared resource and causes unintended consequences
distractors: A race to patch a newly discovered vulnerability
A software update released before discovery
An attack finishing before antivirus scanning
checks.teach: Two operations interfere because each assumes it can use the same state safely. Locking, atomic operations, or safe transaction design can prevent this.
checks.answer: D. Concurrent execution accesses shared state without adequate synchronization, so the result depends on timing or ordering and can become unintended. A race condition is a concurrency flaw, not a synonym for DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service), slow processing, or a race to patch before attackers act.
checks.example: Two checkout requests both see one remaining item before either updates stock. Both complete, selling the same item twice.

setting.object: Two checkout requests both try to buy the last item in stock.
setting.location: Concurrent operations in the store’s application and shared stock record.
setting.purpose: Prevent conflicting operations from producing an unintended result.
setting.action: If both requests read the old stock value before either updates it, timing can cause an incorrect result. Safe synchronization or transactions address the race.
setting.example: Two checkout requests both see one remaining item before either updates stock. Both complete, selling the same item twice.

checks.q: A caller claims to be the help desk and asks for a login code. Hang up and verify through an independently known help-desk number. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: VoIP makes caller-ID spoofing easier
distractors: It is only tailored to organizations
It only targets large organizations
It always uses a real person to call
checks.teach: Voice is the identifying feature. Caller ID is a claim, not proof of identity.
checks.answer: C. VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) makes caller-ID spoofing easier. Vishing is voice phishing: an attacker uses a call or voice message to trick someone into revealing information or performing an action. Calls can be automated, targeted, or broadly distributed; it does not always require a live person.
checks.example: A caller claims to be the help desk and asks for a login code. Hang up and verify through an independently known help-desk number.

setting.object: A caller pretends to be campus IT (Information Technology) and asks for a login code.
setting.location: A phone call or voice message received by an employee.
setting.purpose: Recognize voice-based deception and verify identity through a trusted channel.
setting.action: Vishing uses voice to manipulate the recipient. A displayed caller number can be spoofed and is not proof of identity.
setting.example: A caller claims to be the help desk and asks for a login code. Hang up and verify through an independently known help-desk number.

checks.q: An email claims to come from campus IT but uses a lookalike domain and urgent password language. Preserve the message and inspect headers through the approved reporting process. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Email header
distractors: Attachment
Embedded URL
Email body
checks.teach: Headers provide evidence for investigation. Reading the visible sender label alone is not enough.
checks.answer: D. Email header. Full headers provide routing and sender-related fields such as Received, Return-Path, and authentication results. Compare these with the claimed sender and timestamps. A display name, body, attachment, or embedded URL (Uniform Resource Locator) alone does not establish who sent the message. Some header fields can also be forged; establish trusted receiving-system boundaries.
checks.example: An email claims to come from campus IT (Information Technology) but uses a lookalike domain and urgent password language. Preserve the message and inspect headers through the approved reporting process.

setting.object: An email claims the recipient must urgently reset a university password.
setting.location: The received message, full headers, links, and mail-system records.
setting.purpose: Investigate the claimed sender and request without trusting the display name.
setting.action: Compare routing and authentication evidence, sender domains, timing, and the request with a trusted reporting or verification process.
setting.example: An email claims to come from campus IT (Information Technology) but uses a lookalike domain and urgent password language. Preserve the message and inspect headers through the approved reporting process.

checks.q: Reading script text and decoding an embedded string without running the script is static work. Observing redirects while script executes in an isolated environment is dynamic work. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: JSUnpack
distractors: McAfee Advisor is a source-code compiler
Norton SafeWeb is an offline disassembler
OpenSSL is a browser reputation database
checks.teach: Associate JSUnpack with unpacking suspicious JavaScript. Static versus dynamic describes whether code executes; manual versus automated describes who or what performs the analysis.
checks.answer: C. JSUnpack. It unpacks and analyzes suspicious JavaScript to expose concealed code and URLs. Remember the underlying distinction: static analysis inspects code without running it; dynamic analysis observes execution. JSUnpack also uses emulation, so its capabilities extend beyond static inspection. Firebug is a browser debugger, SiteAdvisor and Safe Web are reputation services, and OpenSSL is a cryptographic toolkit. Static analysis examines code without executing it; dynamic analysis observes execution.
checks.example: Reading script text and decoding an embedded string without running the script is static work. Observing redirects while script executes in an isolated environment is dynamic work.

setting.object: An analyst examines a suspicious web page and its scripts.
setting.location: Page source, an isolated test browser, and website-analysis services.
setting.purpose: Determine what the page does and interpret the evidence behind a safety rating.
setting.action: Static analysis inspects without executing; dynamic analysis observes execution. Manual and automated describe who performs the work; reputation summarizes observations.
setting.example: Reading script text and decoding an embedded string without running the script is static work. Observing redirects while script executes in an isolated environment is dynamic work.

checks.q: A file download needs all bytes in order. TCP can retransmit missing data; TLS is needed separately to protect confidentiality and authenticate the server. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: TCP
distractors: IP
UDP
HTTP
checks.teach: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) handles reliable delivery. It does not itself encrypt your message or prove the other party’s identity.
checks.answer: A. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). Transmission Control Protocol provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery using acknowledgments, retransmissions, sequencing, and a checksum. IP (Internet Protocol) supplies addressing and routing. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)’s reliability and checksum are not confidentiality or cryptographic authentication. HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) security at a different level.
checks.example: A file download needs all bytes in order. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) can retransmit missing data; TLS (Transport Layer Security) is needed separately to protect confidentiality and authenticate the server.

setting.object: A laptop sends file data to a server across a network.
setting.location: The application, transport service, IP (Internet Protocol) network, and local links.
setting.purpose: Understand which layer handles reliable delivery, separate messages, and forwarding.
setting.action: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides separate datagrams without those guarantees; IP (Internet Protocol) forwards packets toward destinations.
setting.example: A file download needs all bytes in order. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) can retransmit missing data; TLS (Transport Layer Security) is needed separately to protect confidentiality and authenticate the server.

checks.q: A legitimate backup triggers a malware alert: false positive. A real malicious download produces no alert: false negative. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: False positive
distractors: False negative
True positive
True negative
checks.teach: Positive means the system says threat. False means that conclusion is wrong.
checks.answer: False positive, also called a Type I error in your notes. A false negative (Type II) occurs when malicious traffic is treated as benign. False positives consume analyst time and can interrupt legitimate work if prevention blocks the traffic; false negatives leave attacks undetected.
checks.example: A legitimate backup triggers a malware alert: false positive. A real malicious download produces no alert: false negative.

setting.object: A monitoring system warns about a network transfer that may be an attack or a legitimate backup.
setting.location: The security alert and the network or host activity that triggered it.
setting.purpose: Decide whether the alert represents a real problem and choose an appropriate response.
setting.action: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) alerts; IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can intervene. Investigated evidence helps tune rules without hiding real attacks or unnecessarily blocking normal work.
setting.example: A legitimate backup triggers a malware alert: false positive. A real malicious download produces no alert: false negative.

checks.q: A timed destructive routine is a logic bomb. An infected workstation waiting for remote instructions is a bot. Both can be dormant, but they are classified by different behavior. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Bot
distractors: Checksum
Ciphertext
Firewall
checks.teach: C2 (Command and Control) means command and control. In this question, the remote server issuing instructions identifies the program as a bot; the collection of controlled devices is a botnet.
checks.answer: Bot. A malicious bot is a program on a compromised device that receives instructions from a command-and-control (C2 (Command and Control)) server. It can wait for a command before carrying out an action. A botnet is a collection of these controlled devices. Distinguish a logic bomb: code activated by a specified condition, such as a date or file deletion. A backdoor provides concealed access.
checks.example: A timed destructive routine is a logic bomb. An infected workstation waiting for remote instructions is a bot. Both can be dormant, but they are classified by different behavior.

setting.object: A malicious program on an infected computer waits for remote instructions.
setting.location: The infected device and a command-and-control server.
setting.purpose: Recognize the program’s remote-control role.
setting.action: A bot receives C2 (Command and Control) commands. A botnet is a collection of controlled devices; a logic bomb is classified by activation on a specified condition.
setting.example: A timed destructive routine is a logic bomb. An infected workstation waiting for remote instructions is a bot. Both can be dormant, but they are classified by different behavior.

checks.q: One group adopts a rule that older nodes reject while another group continues the old rules. Their accepted transaction histories can diverge. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Hard fork
distractors: Checksum
Digital signature
Symmetric key
checks.teach: A protocol disagreement is different from two miners briefly finding competing blocks.
checks.answer: Hard fork is the guide’s intended term. It changes consensus rules incompatibly, so nodes following different rules can maintain different chains. A persistent split depends on participants continuing both histories; a hard fork need not always leave two lasting communities. A soft fork tightens accepted rules compatibly for older nodes.
checks.example: One group adopts a rule that older nodes reject while another group continues the old rules. Their accepted transaction histories can diverge.

setting.object: Two groups follow different rules for accepting blockchain records, or two payments try to spend the same funds.
setting.location: The transaction ledger maintained by participating computers.
setting.purpose: Understand agreement about which valid transaction history is accepted.
setting.action: Validation and consensus resolve competing histories. Incompatible rule changes can produce a hard fork when participants continue separate histories.
setting.example: One group adopts a rule that older nodes reject while another group continues the old rules. Their accepted transaction histories can diverge.

checks.q: A bit flips while a segment is transmitted and the checksum comparison fails. The receiver can discard it; reliable transport may retransmit. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Checksum
distractors: Ciphertext
Public key
Nonce
checks.teach: An error check catches transmission damage. Authenticating malicious changes requires a stronger, trusted construction.
checks.answer: Checksum. The receiver recomputes an error-detection value and compares it with the transmitted value to detect accidental corruption. An ordinary Internet checksum is not SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) and does not defend against an attacker who can alter data and recompute the checksum. Cryptographic integrity requires a suitable authenticated mechanism such as a MAC or signature.
checks.example: A bit flips while a segment is transmitted and the checksum comparison fails. The receiver can discard it; reliable transport may retransmit.

setting.object: A network segment may have been corrupted during transmission.
setting.location: The transmitted data and the receiver’s error-checking calculation.
setting.purpose: Detect accidental changes to the received contents.
setting.action: The receiver recalculates a checksum and compares it with the transmitted value. An ordinary checksum does not authenticate the sender against deliberate changes.
setting.example: A bit flips while a segment is transmitted and the checksum comparison fails. The receiver can discard it; reliable transport may retransmit.

checks.q: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Distribution, coordination, prioritization, and safe testing become easier
distractors: All updates can be installed without testing
Snapshots eliminate the need for backups
Cloud providers automatically patch every customer application
checks.teach: Organize your discussion by the bottleneck each technology reduces. State one benefit and one limitation for each.
checks.answer: More bandwidth speeds patch distribution, although deployments still need scheduling. Cloud-based and centralized management can coordinate updates across fleets, while customers retain responsibilities for their own systems and configurations. Analytics helps inventory systems, prioritize exposure, and detect failed updates. Virtualization supports representative test environments, snapshots, and rollback. Together these reduce transfer, coordination, decision, and testing costs. They do not remove compatibility testing, outages, or zero-day risk.
checks.example: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available.

setting.object: An IT (Information Technology) team must install security updates on many company computers without breaking work.
setting.location: Update distribution, test devices, deployment records, and production systems.
setting.purpose: Repair weaknesses efficiently while verifying that needed services still work.
setting.action: Bandwidth helps distribute updates; centralized services coordinate; analytics prioritizes; virtual machines support testing. Stage changes and verify the results.
setting.example: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available.

checks.q: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Virus needs a host; worm propagates independently; other names describe behavior
distractors: All malware is a virus
Scareware is legitimate antivirus
Backdoors are the same as checksums
checks.teach: Compare how malware spreads, hides, and acts. These categories can overlap: a backdoor may install spyware that includes a keylogger.
checks.answer: A virus attaches to a host file or document and replicates when the host runs; a worm is a standalone program that can propagate across networks. Scareware uses fraudulent alarms to pressure payment or installation. Adware displays unwanted advertising; spyware secretly collects information; a backdoor bypasses normal access controls. In this textbook’s Chapter 2, viruses include program/file viruses and macro viruses, with appender infection and armored concealment techniques: Swiss cheese, split infection, oligomorphic, polymorphic, and metamorphic mutation. Boot-sector viruses are another common category, but the supplied edition emphasizes the preceding list. The guide labels this Ch. 1; the relevant detail is actually Ch. 2, pp. 55–65.
checks.example: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense.

setting.object: An employee opens an infected program or document, or a malicious program spreads between computers.
setting.location: Program files, documents, running software, and networked devices.
setting.purpose: Identify how malicious software propagates and what harmful behavior it performs.
setting.action: A virus attaches to a host; a worm propagates independently. Spyware observes, adware displays ads, scareware deceives with warnings, and a backdoor provides concealed access.
setting.example: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense.

checks.q: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Encryption protects reading; authentication proves origin; obfuscation obscures details
distractors: A hash alone proves the sender
A signature automatically hides the message
Obfuscation always replaces encryption
checks.teach: Ask three separate questions: who can read, who created or approved it, and what details are being obscured?
checks.answer: Confidentiality limits who can read data, usually through encryption. Authentication establishes a claimed identity or data origin through a suitable cryptographic protocol; a digital signature can bind a message to a signing key. Obfuscation makes information or implementation details harder to understand, and the textbook includes it among cryptographic protections. These goals complement one another but do not substitute for one another. Encryption to a recipient’s public key does not by itself identify the sender; an ordinary hash does not authenticate an origin; signing does not encrypt the message. For secrecy plus sender authentication, use a properly designed encrypted and authenticated scheme.
checks.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.

setting.object: A business sends a private document and needs to detect changes or verify its approval.
setting.location: The document, any encrypted representation, its computed digest, and any digital signature.
setting.purpose: Choose the operation that fits confidentiality, content comparison, or origin verification.
setting.action: Encryption hides readable content; a trusted hash comparison checks content; a signature supports verification under a trusted signing key. These operations are not interchangeable.
setting.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.

checks.q: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Large well-distributed outputs make finding collisions computationally difficult
distractors: Collisions are mathematically impossible
Hashing encrypts every input uniquely
All hash algorithms have equal collision resistance
checks.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.
checks.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.
checks.example: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison.

setting.object: A downloaded file is compared with a publisher’s trusted reference digest.
setting.location: The file’s bytes and a program computing a digest from those bytes.
setting.purpose: Detect different contents using a trusted comparison, and distinguish that from sender authentication.
setting.action: A secure hash computes a fixed-length digest. Collisions remain possible but should be hard to find. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) additionally uses a shared secret for message authentication.
setting.example: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison.

checks.q: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Hash links plus validation and consensus create a shared tamper-evident history
distractors: Encryption alone makes every transaction private
A nonce is the owner’s password
Every blockchain must use Bitcoin mining
checks.teach: Hashes connect history; signatures authorize spending; consensus resolves competing histories. None does all three jobs alone.
checks.answer: Transactions are grouped into blocks. A block header commits to transaction data through a Merkle root and includes the previous block’s hash. Altering data changes its hash and breaks later commitments. Nodes validate transactions and consensus determines the accepted history. In Bitcoin, proof of work requires miners to search nonces for a header hash meeting a target; the accepted valid chain has the greatest cumulative work. More confirmations make rewriting history harder under the network’s security assumptions. Benefits include shared auditability and tamper evidence. Costs include proof-of-work energy use, throughput/latency limits, public-data privacy issues, key loss, and difficult correction of erroneous entries. Blockchain is not an absolute guarantee of truth or immutability, and not all blockchains use proof of work.
checks.example: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part.

setting.object: A user transfers digital value to another user without a central ledger operator.
setting.location: Transactions and blocks validated by participating Bitcoin computers.
setting.purpose: Authorize spending, prevent conflicting accepted spends, and maintain an agreed history.
setting.action: Keys authorize spending through signatures; nodes validate transactions; consensus establishes accepted history; incentives support block production.
setting.example: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part.

checks.q: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: A peer-to-peer currency with signature-authorized spending and blockchain consensus
distractors: A coin encrypted with SHA-256 and emailed
A central-bank database with no signatures
An anonymous password shared by all miners
checks.teach: Ownership means the ability to authorize spending under the output’s rules. You transfer spending rights through a transaction; you do not email a secret coin file.
checks.answer: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer digital currency whose transaction history is recorded on a blockchain. A spender authorizes use of earlier unspent transaction outputs by satisfying their spending conditions, typically with a digital signature created using the spender’s private key. A new output specifies conditions for the receiver. Nodes verify authorization and check for double spending; mining orders valid transactions through proof of work. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) contributes to hashing and proof of work, not encryption of a coin. An address is commonly derived from a key or script and is not always the raw public key. Public ledger transparency provides pseudonymity, not guaranteed anonymity. Miners receive a block subsidy and transaction fees as incentives.
checks.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.

setting.object: A user transfers digital value to another user without a central ledger operator.
setting.location: Transactions and blocks validated by participating Bitcoin computers.
setting.purpose: Authorize spending, prevent conflicting accepted spends, and maintain an agreed history.
setting.action: Keys authorize spending through signatures; nodes validate transactions; consensus establishes accepted history; incentives support block production.
setting.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.

checks.q: A hospital considers ransomware risk to patient records. Backups improve recovery, access controls restrict disclosure, and monitoring detects changes. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Keep information private; prevent unauthorized changes; keep services usable by authorized people.
distractors: CPU, Internet, and antivirus
Only encryption strength
The same property under three names
checks.teach: Confidentiality means only permitted people can see the data. Integrity means the data is not changed without permission. Availability means authorized users can get the data or service when needed.
