checks.answer: Confidentiality restricts disclosure, integrity protects against unauthorized alteration, and availability provides access when needed. An asset has value; a vulnerability is a weakness; a threat can cause harm; risk concerns likelihood and impact. Risk responses include accept, avoid, mitigate, and transfer. Controls can be technical, administrative, or physical.
checks.example: A hospital considers ransomware risk to patient records. Backups improve recovery, access controls restrict disclosure, and monitoring detects changes.

setting.object: A school stores private student records and operates a registration service.
setting.location: The records, accounts, applications, and computers used by students and staff.
setting.purpose: Protect privacy, accurate records, and usable services while assessing likely harm.
setting.action: Identify valuable assets, weaknesses, possible threats, and likelihood and impact. Reduce, avoid, accept, or transfer risk according to the action taken.
setting.example: A hospital considers ransomware risk to patient records. Backups improve recovery, access controls restrict disclosure, and monitoring detects changes.

checks.q: A disgruntled staff member has access to payroll. An outside criminal uses a phishing toolkit. The controls must account for both trusted and untrusted access. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Motivation, capability, resources, and access help assess threats
distractors: Zero-day is a job title
Insiders cannot be malicious
Every attacker needs advanced programming skills
checks.teach: Identify who, why, capability, and access rather than assuming one threat always ranks first.
checks.answer: Organized crime often seeks profit; hacktivists pursue ideological goals; nation-state actors may seek espionage or disruption; insiders already have trusted access; script kiddies rely on existing tools; vulnerability brokers sell knowledge. Advanced persistent threats involve sustained, targeted activity. Zero-day describes an unknown or unpatched vulnerability context, not a person. Your notes emphasize social engineering and insiders as pressing concerns; actual priority depends on organizational exposure.
checks.example: A disgruntled staff member has access to payroll. An outside criminal uses a phishing toolkit. The controls must account for both trusted and untrusted access.

setting.object: A company considers both a malicious employee and an outside criminal group.
setting.location: The organization’s accounts, information, services, and existing access.
setting.purpose: Assess what each actor could reach, why they might act, and what resources they have.
setting.action: Compare motivation, capability, resources, and access instead of assuming every attacker has the same opportunities.
setting.example: A disgruntled staff member has access to payroll. An outside criminal uses a phishing toolkit. The controls must account for both trusted and untrusted access.

checks.q: Email filtering, a standard-user account, endpoint monitoring, and recovery procedures protect different points in a phishing incident. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Use multiple safeguards, grant only needed access, vary protection methods, hide unnecessary details, and keep rules understandable.
distractors: Publish all secrets to simplify access
Use only one secret product
Give all users administrator rights
checks.teach: Layering means several protective layers. Limiting means giving only necessary access. Diversity reduces reliance on one kind of protection. Obscurity hides unnecessary information but cannot replace real security. Simplicity keeps controls understandable and manageable.
checks.answer: Layering adds multiple safeguards. Limiting gives only necessary access. Diversity reduces shared failure modes across products or controls. Obscurity hides unnecessary details but cannot be the sole defense. Simplicity makes controls easier to understand and manage. Frameworks and reference architectures organize a security program; some are regulatory, industry-specific, national, or international.
checks.example: Email filtering, a standard-user account, endpoint monitoring, and recovery procedures protect different points in a phishing incident.

setting.object: A store separates payment computers, checks incoming traffic, records device activity, and provides backup network equipment.
setting.location: Network boundaries, staff computers, security records, and the people managing controls.
setting.purpose: Keep the business operating while restricting harmful actions at multiple points.
setting.action: Layer complementary controls, grant necessary access only, collect useful evidence, and plan for growth and device failure. People and procedures must support the tools.
setting.example: Email filtering, a standard-user account, endpoint monitoring, and recovery procedures protect different points in a phishing incident.

checks.q: A retailer inspects gateway traffic, segments payment systems, collects endpoint events, and uses redundant devices to avoid a single outage. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Inspect traffic at controlled entry points, collect useful records, provide backup paths, and plan for growing traffic.
distractors: A perimeter firewall eliminates all endpoint risk
Visibility means capturing only public web pages
Redundancy makes filtering rules unnecessary
checks.teach: A choke point is a controlled place where traffic passes. Visibility means collecting evidence of activity. Availability means keeping services working. Scalability means handling growth. For example, a store checks traffic entering its network, keeps payment computers separate from other systems, records activity on staff devices, and provides a backup network device so one failure does not stop sales.
checks.answer: Use safeguards at both perimeter and endpoint. A choke point is a controlled entry or exit where traffic can be inspected; internal segmentation also matters. Visibility requires useful telemetry at these boundaries and on hosts. Redundancy reduces single points of failure, while scalability supports changing workload. Balance security with business availability, budget, and capacity.
checks.example: A retailer inspects gateway traffic, segments payment systems, collects endpoint events, and uses redundant devices to avoid a single outage.

setting.object: A store separates payment computers, checks incoming traffic, records device activity, and provides backup network equipment.
setting.location: Network boundaries, staff computers, security records, and the people managing controls.
setting.purpose: Keep the business operating while restricting harmful actions at multiple points.
setting.action: Layer complementary controls, grant necessary access only, collect useful evidence, and plan for growth and device failure. People and procedures must support the tools.
setting.example: A retailer inspects gateway traffic, segments payment systems, collects endpoint events, and uses redundant devices to avoid a single outage.

checks.q: An alert-only sensor reports suspicious traffic. An inline prevention rule blocks the same traffic, potentially interrupting legitimate service if the rule is wrong. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts; an IPS can also block or interrupt suspicious activity.
distractors: IDS always blocks packets
IPS always requires AI
An antivirus database makes false negatives impossible
checks.teach: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) stands for Intrusion Detection System. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) stands for Intrusion Prevention System. Detection raises an alert. Prevention can take action to stop activity. Both need careful rules so normal work is not mistaken for an attack.
checks.answer: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) detects suspicious activity and alerts. An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can actively block or disrupt traffic or activity. Either can use signatures, heuristics, behavior, or other techniques; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) does not require AI. Host IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) observes local activity; network controls observe traffic. Tune false positives and false negatives in light of business impact.
checks.example: An alert-only sensor reports suspicious traffic. An inline prevention rule blocks the same traffic, potentially interrupting legitimate service if the rule is wrong.

setting.object: A monitoring system warns about a network transfer that may be an attack or a legitimate backup.
setting.location: The security alert and the network or host activity that triggered it.
setting.purpose: Decide whether the alert represents a real problem and choose an appropriate response.
setting.action: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) alerts; IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can intervene. Investigated evidence helps tune rules without hiding real attacks or unnecessarily blocking normal work.
setting.example: An alert-only sensor reports suspicious traffic. An inline prevention rule blocks the same traffic, potentially interrupting legitimate service if the rule is wrong.

checks.q: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Packet capture stores packet bytes; flow records summarize connections; a proxy handles requests; allowlisting controls which programs run.
distractors: Flow records always include every file
A proxy is the same as PCAP
Allowlisting permits all unknown programs
checks.teach: Packet capture records observed packet contents within recording limits. Flow records summarize who communicated, when, and how much. A proxy receives and forwards application requests while applying rules. Application allowlisting prevents unapproved programs from running. These are four different jobs.
checks.answer: Full PCAP (Packet Capture) records packet bytes within capture limits, useful for detailed reconstruction; encrypted payloads remain encrypted without suitable keys. Flow records summarize conversations such as endpoints, times, ports, and byte counts. A proxy mediates application requests and can enforce policy and log activity. Application allowlisting permits approved software and restricts other execution. These controls complement rather than replace one another.
checks.example: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events.

setting.object: An analyst needs evidence about traffic leaving a company laptop.
setting.location: A monitored network link, packet captures, connection summaries, and proxy records.
setting.purpose: Choose evidence that can answer who communicated, when, how much, and potentially what was carried.
setting.action: PCAP (Packet Capture) records observed packet bytes; flow records summarize connections. Mirrors and taps determine what the sensor can see. A proxy handles requests; allowlisting controls software execution.
setting.example: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events.

checks.q: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: They consume connection resources and deny legitimate access
distractors: All DoS attacks require a giant botnet
Slowloris encrypts a database
A SYN flood is simply a race condition
checks.teach: Bandwidth floods and application connection exhaustion stress different resources. Match mitigation to the bottleneck.
checks.answer: Denial of service exhausts resources or disrupts access; distributed DoS (Denial of Service) uses multiple sources. A SYN flood abuses half-open TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection state. Slowloris holds many HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) connections with incomplete, slow requests and may work from few sources. Mitigations include upstream filtering, rate and connection limits, appropriate timeouts, SYN protections, and capacity planning. DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) can distract responders but is not always a distraction or a race condition.
checks.example: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern.

setting.object: Customers cannot use a website because an attacker occupies its connection-handling capacity.
setting.location: The web server and the network or application connections it handles.
setting.purpose: Keep the service usable for legitimate customers.
setting.action: SYN floods target connection setup; Slowloris holds web requests incomplete. Match mitigation to the exhausted resource rather than assuming every attack needs enormous bandwidth.
setting.example: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern.

checks.q: A search value must remain a SQL parameter. A comment displayed on a page must remain text or sanitized allowed HTML rather than executable script. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: SQLi changes query interpretation; XSS executes script in the browser
distractors: Both are prevented by antivirus alone
XSS always takes full control of the application server
Prepared statements alone prevent every XSS flaw
checks.teach: Ask where the injected content is interpreted: database query engine or victim browser. XSS (Cross Site Scripting) is not automatically full server control.
checks.answer: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection makes untrusted input influence database query structure. Parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL (Structured Query Language) commands; least-privilege database accounts limit harm. XSS (Cross Site Scripting) causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a user’s browser in a trusted site’s context. Use context-aware output encoding, safe APIs, and appropriate sanitization for allowed HTML (Hypertext Markup Language). Input validation supports both but is insufficient alone. WebGoat is a deliberately vulnerable teaching application. Neither attack is limited to one operating system.
checks.example: A search value must remain a SQL (Structured Query Language) parameter. A comment displayed on a page must remain text or sanitized allowed HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) rather than executable script.

setting.object: A website accepts user input, queries a database, and displays results in a browser.
setting.location: The application, database query, browser output, and potentially the program’s memory.
setting.purpose: Keep input from becoming unintended instructions at the relevant interpreter or memory boundary.
setting.action: Parameterized queries address SQL (Structured Query Language) injection; safe output handling addresses XSS (Cross Site Scripting); bounds checking and memory safety address buffer overflows. The flaws affect different places.
setting.example: A search value must remain a SQL (Structured Query Language) parameter. A comment displayed on a page must remain text or sanitized allowed HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) rather than executable script.

checks.q: An urgent campus-password message aimed at named students is targeted phishing. A phone request for login codes is vishing. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Targeting and communication channel distinguish the methods
distractors: Smishing uses only voice calls
Spear phishing is always random
419 scams provide guaranteed legitimate rewards
checks.teach: Channel, targeting, and pretext distinguish these related attacks.
checks.answer: Phishing uses deceptive communication to elicit information or action. Spear phishing targets particular recipients using tailored context. Smishing uses SMS; vishing uses voice. A 419 or advance-fee scam promises a benefit to obtain money or sensitive data upfront. Scareware creates false security urgency. Verify requests through independent trusted channels and report suspicious messages.
checks.example: An urgent campus-password message aimed at named students is targeted phishing. A phone request for login codes is vishing.

setting.object: A person receives a convincing message promising a reward, or a website’s visible page is changed without permission.
setting.location: Email, text messages, calls, payment requests, or published website content.
setting.purpose: Distinguish manipulation of people from unauthorized changes to website content.
setting.action: Social-engineering categories depend on targeting and delivery channel. Advance-fee fraud asks for payment first; defacement changes the visible site.
setting.example: An urgent campus-password message aimed at named students is targeted phishing. A phone request for login codes is vishing.

checks.q: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Structured testing and social-engineering simulation reveal technical and human weaknesses
distractors: SET is a hash algorithm
Patching alone prevents every fake-login attack
A captured password always means code executed on the host
checks.teach: Explain the weakness, business consequence, evidence, and defense. Exact tool-menu commands are not the stated exam priority.
checks.answer: Metasploit organizes authorized security testing through exploit, payload, auxiliary, and post-exploitation capabilities. SET (Social Engineer Toolkit) is a separate TrustedSec social-engineering toolkit that can integrate with Metasploit; it is not simply a Metasploit module. The credential-harvesting lab demonstrates how user trust can disclose credentials without a software exploit. Prevent with training, filtering, phishing-resistant MFA (Multi Factor Authentication), and login monitoring. If credentials are disclosed, report, reset affected secrets from a trusted device, revoke sessions, and investigate related access.
checks.example: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions.

setting.object: A staff member enters a test password into a cloned login page.
setting.location: The employee’s browser and a credential-collection page in the authorized lab.
setting.purpose: Understand how a convincing page can obtain credentials through user interaction.
setting.action: The form submits the entered information to the collecting system. This alone does not prove malicious code ran on the employee’s computer.
setting.example: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions.

checks.q: The lab’s isolated victim records test keystrokes. An organization should investigate the endpoint and account access rather than assume HTTPS prevented disclosure. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: The endpoint can capture keystrokes before transport encryption
distractors: HTTPS disables all keyboard monitoring
All keyloggers are network routers
Only encrypted keystrokes can be logged
checks.teach: Protection during transmission does not protect the moment data is typed on a compromised device.
checks.answer: A keylogger records input on the endpoint, often before TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts it for transport. Software variants may intercept input APIs, run with elevated privileges, or observe forms; hardware variants can sit between keyboard and computer. Not every keylogger requires process injection or admin rights. Defend with endpoint monitoring, least privilege, updates, application controls, physical inspection where appropriate, and phishing-resistant authentication. Transport encryption alone cannot secure a compromised endpoint.
checks.example: The lab’s isolated victim records test keystrokes. An organization should investigate the endpoint and account access rather than assume HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) prevented disclosure.

setting.object: An employee types a password on a computer with a software or hardware keylogger.
setting.location: The device’s input path, before transport encryption protects a web connection.
setting.purpose: Understand how information can be captured at the device even when HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) is used.
setting.action: A keylogger records keystrokes. Transport encryption does not protect input already observed on a compromised endpoint; physical and software controls address different variants.
setting.example: The lab’s isolated victim records test keystrokes. An organization should investigate the endpoint and account access rather than assume HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) prevented disclosure.

checks.q: A business tests a browser update in a representative VM, deploys to a pilot group, monitors compatibility, then expands rollout. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Test updates, reduce services and privileges, enforce controls, and verify
distractors: Disable all production firewalls to match a lab
Allow daily work with administrator rights
Assume automatic updates can never fail
checks.teach: Reduce attack surface and limit damage before an incident. Verify that deployed controls actually work.
checks.answer: Inventory assets, apply tested updates, use standard-user accounts, remove unnecessary services, enable appropriate endpoint firewall and protection, restrict software execution, and monitor changes. A patch workflow downloads, tests, pilots, schedules, deploys, and verifies, with rollback planning. NAC (Network Access Control) checks access posture; GPO (Group Policy Object) distributes domain policy. Patching addresses known vulnerabilities but does not eliminate zero-days. Legacy tool names in notes are historical examples, not a current shopping list.
checks.example: A business tests a browser update in a representative VM (Virtual Machine), deploys to a pilot group, monitors compatibility, then expands rollout.

setting.object: An administrator configures a staff laptop before allowing normal work and network access.
setting.location: The device’s accounts, operating-system settings, services, updates, and local security controls.
setting.purpose: Reduce unnecessary exposure and enforce appropriate access and execution rules.
setting.action: Use standard accounts, patch software, disable unneeded services, configure host protections, and verify required settings. NAC (Network Access Control), GPO (Group Policy Object), endpoint firewalls, and HIPS (Host Intrusion Prevention System) perform different jobs.
setting.example: A business tests a browser update in a representative VM (Virtual Machine), deploys to a pilot group, monitors compatibility, then expands rollout.

checks.q: An Office process starts unusual PowerShell, followed by a new outbound connection and credential access. Build a timeline, identify affected hosts, preserve evidence, and contain according to the incident plan. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Correlate process, network, identity, and file evidence into a timeline
distractors: Treat all PowerShell use as proof of compromise
Sandbox means the same as PowerShell
Exfiltration means installing a software update
checks.teach: Separate the tools, techniques, evidence, and outcomes. Seeing a tool name alone does not establish malicious intent.
checks.answer: Correlate host process events, network connections, authentication logs, and file changes. A SOC (Security Operations Center) coordinates monitoring and response. EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) supplies endpoint detection and response evidence. Reconnaissance gathers information; privilege escalation increases rights; credential dumping extracts stored authentication material; SMB (Server Message Block) commonly supports network file sharing. Process hollowing replaces or maps malicious code into another process context. PowerShell is an administration shell and scripting environment; a sandbox is an isolated execution environment. DLL (Dynamic Link Library) means Dynamic Link Library. Infiltration gains entry; exfiltration removes information.
checks.example: An Office process starts unusual PowerShell, followed by a new outbound connection and credential access. Build a timeline, identify affected hosts, preserve evidence, and contain according to the incident plan.

setting.object: A staff login is followed by an unusual program launch and an outbound transfer.
setting.location: Account logs, endpoint process and file events, and network records.
setting.purpose: Reconstruct related events, assess affected systems, and decide containment actions.
setting.action: Correlate timestamps and details rather than assuming one alert proves all data was stolen. Check clock accuracy, record coverage, and how long logs were retained.
setting.example: An Office process starts unusual PowerShell, followed by a new outbound connection and credential access. Build a timeline, identify affected hosts, preserve evidence, and contain according to the incident plan.

checks.q: A tester uses an isolated guest network to observe activity, takes a baseline snapshot, and restores the guest after the exercise. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Isolation and reproducible guest states support controlled testing
distractors: NAT and internal network are identical
A snapshot replaces every backup
Disabling production firewalls is a hardening step
checks.teach: Explain why a control is disabled in a demonstration and why a real organization would enforce it.
checks.answer: The host runs VirtualBox and the guest operating systems. The lab uses Kali and Windows 7 guests with an internal network for guest-to-guest tests and NAT (Network Address Translation) for controlled Internet access during setup. Internal networking does not make the entire host immune; additional adapters and sharing features affect exposure. Static guest addresses support predictable connectivity. Snapshots help restore a known lab state but do not replace independent backups. Disabling a guest firewall was an intentionally weakened lab condition, not a production hardening practice.
checks.example: A tester uses an isolated guest network to observe activity, takes a baseline snapshot, and restores the guest after the exercise.

setting.object: A student runs intentionally vulnerable guest machines for a controlled lab.
setting.location: Virtualization software, guest operating systems, virtual network adapters, and saved states.
setting.purpose: Keep experiments controlled and distinguish the guest environment from the physical host.
setting.action: Hypervisors manage guests; network settings affect reachability; snapshots help restore states. Containers, VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure), and uncontrolled VM (Virtual Machine) growth have different boundaries and management concerns.
setting.example: A tester uses an isolated guest network to observe activity, takes a baseline snapshot, and restores the guest after the exercise.

checks.q: A site’s source includes a hidden redirect. An analyst reviews it, consults reputation evidence, and examines behavior in an approved sandbox. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Combine source inspection, isolated behavior observation, and reputation evidence
distractors: A familiar brand proves a page is safe
Automated always means static
A clean reputation scan proves no new malware exists
checks.teach: A known domain and a clean reputation report are evidence, not guarantees.
checks.answer: Static work inspects HTML (Hypertext Markup Language), scripts, redirects, and embedded references without execution. Dynamic work observes behavior in an isolated environment, including processes, files, registry, and traffic. Reputation checks compare against previous reports. Automation is fast but can miss new threats; manual investigation provides context but takes skill and time. A legitimate site can be compromised. Firebug, Malzilla, Wepawet, JSUnpack, SiteAdvisor, and Safe Web are course-era examples.
checks.example: A site’s source includes a hidden redirect. An analyst reviews it, consults reputation evidence, and examines behavior in an approved sandbox.

setting.object: An analyst examines a suspicious web page and its scripts.
setting.location: Page source, an isolated test browser, and website-analysis services.
setting.purpose: Determine what the page does and interpret the evidence behind a safety rating.
setting.action: Static analysis inspects without executing; dynamic analysis observes execution. Manual and automated describe who performs the work; reputation summarizes observations.
setting.example: A site’s source includes a hidden redirect. An analyst reviews it, consults reputation evidence, and examines behavior in an approved sandbox.

checks.q: A document can be hashed for comparison, signed to show approval, and encrypted for its intended reader. These operations have separate roles. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Encrypt for secrecy, hash for comparison, sign for verifiable authorization
distractors: Decrypt SHA-256 to recover the message
Use a bare hash to prove sender identity
Signing automatically encrypts the whole document
checks.teach: Choose the operation by the required property rather than calling every cryptographic output ciphertext.
checks.answer: Encryption protects content confidentiality and is reversible with the correct key. Hashing produces a deterministic fixed-length digest with no intended inverse. A signature uses a private signing key and is checked with a corresponding public key to authenticate authorized data and detect alteration. A bare hash has no secret and does not prove origin. HMAC (Hash based Message Authentication Code) combines a secret key and hash for integrity and shared-key authentication; it is not encryption and does not provide the same public verification as a signature.
checks.example: A document can be hashed for comparison, signed to show approval, and encrypted for its intended reader. These operations have separate roles.

setting.object: A business sends a private document and needs to detect changes or verify its approval.
setting.location: The document, any encrypted representation, its computed digest, and any digital signature.
setting.purpose: Choose the operation that fits confidentiality, content comparison, or origin verification.
setting.action: Encryption hides readable content; a trusted hash comparison checks content; a signature supports verification under a trusted signing key. These operations are not interchangeable.
setting.example: A document can be hashed for comparison, signed to show approval, and encrypted for its intended reader. These operations have separate roles.

checks.q: Alice wants only Bob to read a message and wants Bob to verify her approval. She protects it for Bob and signs it using her own signing key. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Encrypt for Bob using Bob’s public key; Alice signs using her private key, and Bob verifies using Alice’s trusted public key.
distractors: Encrypt with sender public key for only Bob to read
Share all private keys for authentication
Use receiver private key on the sender’s machine
checks.teach: For confidentiality, use the recipient’s public encryption key so the recipient’s private key can decrypt. For a signature, the sender uses the sender’s private signing key; others verify with the corresponding trusted public key. The private keys remain secret.
checks.answer: Symmetric encryption shares one secret for encryption and decryption and is efficient for bulk data. Public-key encryption uses the recipient’s public key and recipient’s private key to decrypt. Signing uses the sender’s private key and verification uses the sender’s public key. Verify the binding between a public key and a claimed identity. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is symmetric; RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) belong to asymmetric families. DES and 3DES are historical course examples, not preferred new-system choices.
checks.example: Alice wants only Bob to read a message and wants Bob to verify her approval. She protects it for Bob and signs it using her own signing key.

setting.object: Alice sends Bob a confidential document and may also sign it.
setting.location: Alice’s and Bob’s applications, cryptographic keys, the document, and any signature.
setting.purpose: Keep the contents readable by the intended recipient and independently verify signed content.
setting.action: Public-key encryption for Bob uses Bob’s public key and corresponding private decryption key. Alice signs with her private signing key; verification uses her trusted public key. Hybrid systems combine public-key techniques with symmetric data protection.

checks.q: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Choose e coprime to φ(n), then d as its modular inverse
distractors: Choose e equal to φ(n)
Use addition instead of modular exponentiation
Make d public and hide e
checks.teach: The private exponent reverses the public exponent modulo n for correctly constructed RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman). Real implementations require safe key sizes and padding.
checks.answer: For distinct primes p and q, n=pq and φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1). Choose e with gcd(e,φ(n))=1 and choose d so ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n). Textbook notation may use m for φ(n). Classroom encryption is c=m^e mod n and decryption is m=c^d mod n. With p=5, q=11, n=55, φ=40, e=3, d=27: message 7 gives ciphertext 13 and decrypts to 7. The notes’ condition using e and n is incorrect; coprimality with φ(n) is essential. Small unpadded examples teach arithmetic and are not secure deployments.
checks.example: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7.

setting.example: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7.

checks.q: Changing one transaction changes the Merkle root, then its block header hash and the descendants’ required links. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: The nonce is varied to search for a qualifying hash; the Merkle root summarizes the transactions; the previous-block hash links to earlier history.
distractors: Nonce is the receiver’s private key
Merkle root stores every private password
Prior hash encrypts all previous transactions
checks.teach: A nonce is a search value. The Merkle root is computed from transaction hashes. The previous-block hash identifies the earlier block being built upon. These values support different parts of the block structure.
checks.answer: A proof-of-work nonce is a value miners vary while searching for a block-header hash meeting a target. A Merkle root commits to the block’s transactions using a tree of hashes. The previous-block hash links a block to its predecessor. Altering a transaction changes its commitment and invalidates later links unless recomputed. A toy rehash demonstration is not the full security model: distributed validation and cumulative proof of work make rewriting accepted history difficult.
checks.example: Changing one transaction changes the Merkle root, then its block header hash and the descendants’ required links.

setting.purpose: Summarize included transactions and make changes to linked history detectable.
setting.action: A Merkle root commits to transactions; a proof checks inclusion under that root. The previous-block hash links history; a proof-of-work nonce is varied during the mining search.
setting.example: Changing one transaction changes the Merkle root, then its block header hash and the descendants’ required links.

checks.q: An owner attempts to spend the same output twice. Both signatures could be valid, but both transactions cannot be accepted in one valid history. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Signatures authorize, consensus orders, and rewards motivate participation
distractors: Hashing alone prevents all double spending
All Bitcoin addresses guarantee anonymity
Miners can authorize spending anyone’s coins
checks.teach: Authorization does not establish which of two conflicting authorized spends came first; network agreement addresses that ordering problem.
checks.answer: Signatures demonstrate authorization to spend. Nodes check spending rules, including whether an output is unspent. Consensus orders transactions so competing spends do not both become accepted history. A block subsidy and fees incentivize miners. Public records use addresses or spending scripts rather than mandatory civil identities, but linked transactions can reveal relationships. This is pseudonymity. Nakamoto’s paper contrasts verification by cryptographic proof with the reversal costs, mediation, and trust demands of financial intermediaries.
checks.example: An owner attempts to spend the same output twice. Both signatures could be valid, but both transactions cannot be accepted in one valid history.

checks.q: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP routing. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream with recovery; UDP sends separate messages without those guarantees; IP forwards packets toward destinations.
distractors: IP guarantees every byte in order
UDP is only allowed on private networks
TCP stands for Transportation Control Protocol
checks.teach: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) puts received bytes in order and retransmits missing data when possible. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sends individual messages called datagrams without automatically recovering missing messages or putting them in order. IP (Internet Protocol) handles addressing and forwarding packets between networks; best effort means it does not promise delivery.
checks.answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides a reliable ordered byte stream, using SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for conventional connection establishment. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides datagrams without TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)-style delivery or ordering guarantees and is useful where applications tolerate loss or implement their own recovery. Both operate at the transport layer. IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and routes packets at the network layer with best-effort delivery. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is not restricted to private networks, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does not guarantee timeliness or encryption. Packet lengths can vary.
checks.example: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP (Internet Protocol) routing.

setting.example: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP (Internet Protocol) routing.

checks.q: A name resolves unexpectedly, so an analyst checks DNS evidence and validation. Separate authentication logs and packet metadata help establish the incident timeline. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: DNS looks up names; SNMP manages devices; ICMP carries network diagnostic/control messages; FTP transfers files; SMTP sends mail; POP retrieves mail.
distractors: DNSSEC encrypts every website
FTP always uses port 20 for all traffic
ICMP is a mail retrieval service
checks.teach: Each protocol defines rules for a different communication task. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) adds authentication of signed DNS (Domain Name System) data, not encryption of ordinary queries. Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) does not encrypt its transfers. A protocol’s name alone does not mean its traffic is confidential.
checks.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names and other records; poisoning supplies false resolution information. DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) authenticates signed DNS (Domain Name System) data and integrity when correctly validated, without encrypting ordinary DNS (Domain Name System) queries. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) monitors and manages devices; v3 supports stronger protection. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) carries network control and diagnostic messages, including ping. Traditional FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transfers files without encryption: port 21 controls, port 20 is traditionally active-mode data, while passive mode negotiates data ports. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail and POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves it. Wireshark analyzes packets; log correlation helps investigation.
checks.example: A name resolves unexpectedly, so an analyst checks DNS (Domain Name System) evidence and validation. Separate authentication logs and packet metadata help establish the incident timeline.

distractors: Every matching SSID proves the same operator

An evil-twin wireless access point can imitate a familiar SSID and lure users; a Wi-Fi assessment device can demonstrate these risks but cannot automatically decrypt all nearby secure traffic. A captive portal presents network-access or acceptance steps; its appearance alone does not establish legitimacy. Verify the network and destination, and use authenticated secure protocols.

checks.q: A lost powered-off encrypted laptop needs storage protection. A compromised running session exposes data in use, so disk encryption alone is insufficient. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Full-disk encryption protects stored data when the keys remain protected.
distractors: Steganography always encrypts content
A TPM prevents every software exploit
Forward secrecy means keys never change
checks.teach: Full-disk encryption protects data saved on the drive. It does not prevent every attack after the device is unlocked. Other Chapter 3 concepts have separate definition questions, including steganography, forward secrecy, TPM (Trusted Platform Module), HSM (Hardware Security Module), and stream and block ciphers.
checks.answer: Steganography hides the existence of data; encryption hides readable content. ROT13 is a substitution cipher, and XOR gives 0 for equal input bits and 1 for different bits. Stream ciphers process streams; block ciphers process fixed-size blocks. Diffusion spreads a plaintext change through the output; confusion obscures the relation between key and ciphertext. Secure randomness and key management matter. Diffie-Hellman establishes a shared secret; ephemeral exchanges can support forward secrecy when used correctly. Downgrade attacks force weaker options. TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and HSM (Hardware Security Module) protect cryptographic operations and keys; full-disk encryption protects stored data. Resource, power, and latency constraints influence implementation choices.
checks.example: A lost powered-off encrypted laptop needs storage protection. A compromised running session exposes data in use, so disk encryption alone is insufficient.

distractors: A successful ping proves every application is healthy
SNMP community strings always encrypt traffic
DNSSEC makes all returned websites trustworthy
checks.teach: A DNS (Domain Name System) lookup investigates name resolution. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) can report managed device status. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) messages help diagnose reachability or delivery problems. Each gives only part of the evidence; none proves every application is working correctly.
checks.answer: Naming, management statistics, and reachability are different questions. A single successful diagnostic does not prove the whole service is healthy.
checks.example: A device answers ping but its web application fails. The network evidence establishes only part of the service path, so application logs and connection tests are needed.

checks.q: Why does sensor placement determine what defenders can see?
checks.correct: The sensor sees only traffic that actually reaches its monitored link or copied traffic feed.
distractors: The busiest link reveals every network action

checks.answer: A sensor cannot inspect traffic it never receives. Define the visibility question before selecting its network location.
checks.example: A gateway sensor sees Internet traffic but not two servers talking locally on another switch. An internal mirror or other telemetry may be needed.

checks.q: How do Type I Type II containers VDI and VM sprawl differ?

cloze.q: SHA-256 produces a digest containing _____ bits.
cloze.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.
cloze.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.

cloze.q: The handshake order is SYN, _____, ACK.
distractors: FIN

cloze.answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides a reliable ordered byte stream, using SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for conventional connection establishment. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides datagrams without TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)-style delivery or ordering guarantees and is useful where applications tolerate loss or implement their own recovery. Both operate at the transport layer. IP (Internet Protocol) addresses and routes packets at the network layer with best-effort delivery. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is not restricted to private networks, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) does not guarantee timeliness or encryption. Packet lengths can vary.
cloze.teach: Reliability, latency tradeoffs, and routing are separate design concerns.
cloze.example: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP (Internet Protocol) routing.

Software variants may intercept input APIs, run with elevated privileges, or observe forms; hardware variants can sit between keyboard and computer. sorts.answer: Sender hashes the message → Sender signs with sender private key → Recipient receives message and signature → Recipient verifies using sender public key
sorts.teach: Ask three separate questions: who can read, who created or approved it, and what details are being obscured?
sorts.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.

setting.object: A business sends a private document and needs to detect changes or verify its approval.
setting.location: The document, any encrypted representation, its computed digest, and any digital signature.
setting.purpose: Choose the operation that fits confidentiality, content comparison, or origin verification.
setting.action: Encryption hides readable content; a trusted hash comparison checks content; a signature supports verification under a trusted signing key. These operations are not interchangeable.
setting.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.

items: Owner prepares spend to recipient conditions
Nodes verify authorization and unspent inputs
Valid transaction enters accepted block history
sorts.answer: Owner prepares spend to recipient conditions → Owner authorizes with private-key signature → Nodes verify authorization and unspent inputs → Valid transaction enters accepted block history
sorts.teach: Ownership means the ability to authorize spending under the output’s rules. You transfer spending rights through a transaction; you do not email a secret coin file.
sorts.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.

setting.object: A user transfers digital value to another user without a central ledger operator.
setting.location: Transactions and blocks validated by participating Bitcoin computers.
setting.purpose: Authorize spending, prevent conflicting accepted spends, and maintain an agreed history.
setting.action: Keys authorize spending through signatures; nodes validate transactions; consensus establishes accepted history; incentives support block production.
setting.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.

items: Correlate host network and identity events
sorts.answer: Collect and preserve available telemetry → Correlate host network and identity events → Identify scope and business impact → Recommend containment and recovery
sorts.teach: Separate the tools, techniques, evidence, and outcomes. Seeing a tool name alone does not establish malicious intent.
sorts.example: An Office process starts unusual PowerShell, followed by a new outbound connection and credential access. Build a timeline, identify affected hosts, preserve evidence, and contain according to the incident plan.

setting.action: Identify valuable assets, weaknesses, possible threats, and likelihood and impact. Reduce, avoid, accept, or transfer risk according to the action taken.
setting.example: A hospital considers ransomware risk to patient records. Backups improve recovery, access controls restrict disclosure, and monitoring detects changes.

vocab.answer: Intrusion Detection System. A control that detects suspicious activity and raises alerts. Detection does not necessarily block the activity.
vocab.teach: A control that detects suspicious activity and raises alerts. Detection does not necessarily block the activity.

Internet Detection Standard

setting.object: A monitoring system warns about a network transfer that may be an attack or a legitimate backup.
setting.location: The security alert and the network or host activity that triggered it.
setting.purpose: Decide whether the alert represents a real problem and choose an appropriate response.
setting.action: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) alerts; IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can intervene. Investigated evidence helps tune rules without hiding real attacks or unnecessarily blocking normal work.
setting.example: A legitimate backup triggers a malware alert: false positive. A real malicious download produces no alert: false negative.

vocab.answer: Intrusion Prevention System. A control that can actively prevent or disrupt suspicious activity, with tuning needed to avoid blocking legitimate work.
vocab.teach: A control that can actively prevent or disrupt suspicious activity, with tuning needed to avoid blocking legitimate work.

Internet Policy Standard

corrections: The second guide could not select a job title without the textbook. Printed page 6 explicitly supports security administrator.
Social-Engineer Toolkit uses deception, including cloned login pages, to capture information through user interaction.
An outbound shell may pass permissive packet filters. Application proxies enforce protocol and destination policies; protection depends on configuration and inspection.
A bot receives remote C2 commands. A logic bomb activates when a specified condition occurs; a botnet is a collection of controlled devices.
JSUnpack unpacks suspicious JavaScript and includes emulation. Static inspection and dynamic execution are distinct analysis techniques.
The guide points at Chapter 1. Detailed virus types in this edition are Chapter 2, pp. 55–65.
Script runs in a victim browser in the site context. It does not inherently grant full application-server control.
Fixed-length digests are not guaranteed unique. Plain hashes do not establish sender identity.
Recipient keys protect confidentiality; sender keys sign and verify. Signing is not generally described as encrypting with a private key.
Choose e coprime to φ(n), not merely coprime to n. Use ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n).
Transmission Control Protocol provides reliability, not encryption. Its Internet checksum is not a cryptographic SHA digest.
MFA reduces password-only compromise but does not stop every phishing or session attack. HTTPS cannot protect data already exposed on a compromised endpoint.
Pseudonymity is not anonymity. Prefer greatest cumulative proof of work to a simplistic longest-by-block-count rule.
IPS does not require AI. Allowlisting is a control concept, not inherently obsolete.
Professor guide estimates 15 T/F, 20 MC, 10 blanks, 5–7 discussions. October 15 notes give ranges of 10–15, 20–25, 10–12, 5–7. Neither is an exact promise.
All eight lecture decks are now directly reviewed. Lectures 2–4 were recovered from PPTs_export.zip; the duplicate Lecture 3 copy has identical extracted slide/note text.
AES uses 128-bit blocks and 128/192/256-bit keys with total rounds 10/12/14. Keep block size separate from key size and the textbook’s middle-round count.
TPM and HSM are different categories. Hardware is not immune to every implementation or firmware attack.
SFTP is over SSH; FTPS adds TLS to FTP. Plain NTP is not automatically authenticated. S/MIME capability depends on the client and key setup.
Old screenshots, prices, percentages, vendor support schedules, and legal penalties are not presented as current facts or required memorization.
The lecture’s 65-bit hexadecimal phrase is incorrect. A SHA-256 digest has 256 bits, typically displayed as 64 hexadecimal characters.

primer.meaning: A computer or device on which programs run, such as a laptop or server.
A server provides a service; a client requests it. One device can perform both roles.
The OS (Operating System) manages the device’s resources. An application performs a task using those resources.
A network connects devices. A protocol gives rules for their communication.
A packet carries data. Its header carries control information; its payload is the carried content, which can itself contain another layer’s header.
An IP (Internet Protocol) address identifies a network endpoint; a port helps identify a transport service or conversation.
A vulnerability is a weakness. An exploit takes advantage of it. A payload is the action or code delivered or run.
Authentication checks a claimed identity. Authorization decides what that identity may do.
A firewall enforces communication rules. Detection identifies suspicious activity; an alert needs investigation.
A key controls a cryptographic operation. A hash is a digest for comparison. A signature provides verifiable authorization or origin under a trusted key.
A public key may be distributed. Its corresponding private key must stay secret. Which person’s key you use depends on the goal.
Explain what information, money, service, or trust is at risk, and why your proposed defense addresses it.
A transaction records a transfer or other event. A ledger is the record of those events.
A block groups records and control information. A blockchain links blocks using cryptographic commitments to earlier history.
Validation checks the rules. Consensus is how participants agree on an accepted history despite competing or faulty participants.
Distributed work or storage is spread across systems. Decentralized authority is spread across decision makers. A distributed system can still be centrally controlled.

discussions.title: Why patching becomes easier
discussions.q: How do bandwidth, cloud computing, big data/analytics, and virtualization alleviate security-update pressure?
discussions.answer: More bandwidth speeds patch distribution, although deployments still need scheduling. Cloud-based and centralized management can coordinate updates across fleets, while customers retain responsibilities for their own systems and configurations. Analytics helps inventory systems, prioritize exposure, and detect failed updates. Virtualization supports representative test environments, snapshots, and rollback. Together these reduce transfer, coordination, decision, and testing costs. They do not remove compatibility testing, outages, or zero-day risk.
discussions.teach: Organize your discussion by the bottleneck each technology reduces. State one benefit and one limitation for each.
discussions.example: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available.
discussions.correct: Distribution, coordination, prioritization, and safe testing become easier
distractors: All updates can be installed without testing
Snapshots eliminate the need for backups
Cloud providers automatically patch every customer application

discussions.title: Viruses and other malware
discussions.q: What are the major types of computer viruses, and how do virus, worm, scareware, adware, spyware, and backdoor differ?
discussions.answer: A virus attaches to a host file or document and replicates when the host runs; a worm is a standalone program that can propagate across networks. Scareware uses fraudulent alarms to pressure payment or installation. Adware displays unwanted advertising; spyware secretly collects information; a backdoor bypasses normal access controls. In this textbook’s Chapter 2, viruses include program/file viruses and macro viruses, with appender infection and armored concealment techniques: Swiss cheese, split infection, oligomorphic, polymorphic, and metamorphic mutation. Boot-sector viruses are another common category, but the supplied edition emphasizes the preceding list. The guide labels this Ch. 1; the relevant detail is actually Ch. 2, pp. 55–65.
discussions.teach: Compare how malware spreads, hides, and acts. These categories can overlap: a backdoor may install spyware that includes a keylogger.
discussions.example: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense.
discussions.correct: Virus needs a host; worm propagates independently; other names describe behavior
distractors: All malware is a virus
Scareware is legitimate antivirus
Backdoors are the same as checksums
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
discussions.goal: Explain Viruses and other malware in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.

discussions.title: Confidentiality authentication obfuscation
discussions.q: How do confidentiality, authentication, and obfuscation correlate in cryptographic applications?
discussions.answer: Confidentiality limits who can read data, usually through encryption. Authentication establishes a claimed identity or data origin through a suitable cryptographic protocol; a digital signature can bind a message to a signing key. Obfuscation makes information or implementation details harder to understand, and the textbook includes it among cryptographic protections. These goals complement one another but do not substitute for one another. Encryption to a recipient’s public key does not by itself identify the sender; an ordinary hash does not authenticate an origin; signing does not encrypt the message. For secrecy plus sender authentication, use a properly designed encrypted and authenticated scheme.
discussions.teach: Ask three separate questions: who can read, who created or approved it, and what details are being obscured?
discussions.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.
discussions.correct: Encryption protects reading; authentication proves origin; obfuscation obscures details
distractors: A hash alone proves the sender
A signature automatically hides the message
Obfuscation always replaces encryption
refs: direct lecture review; see topic coverage
rubric: Explain why obfuscation alone is insufficient

discussions.title: Collision resistance
discussions.q: Hash algorithms are naturally resistant to hash collisions. Why?
discussions.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm)-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.
discussions.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.
discussions.example: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison.
discussions.correct: Large well-distributed outputs make finding collisions computationally difficult
distractors: Collisions are mathematically impossible
Hashing encrypts every input uniquely
All hash algorithms have equal collision resistance

discussions.title: Blockchain mechanics and tradeoffs
discussions.q: How does blockchain work? What are its pros and cons?
discussions.answer: Transactions are grouped into blocks. A block header commits to transaction data through a Merkle root and includes the previous block’s hash. Altering data changes its hash and breaks later commitments. Nodes validate transactions and consensus determines the accepted history. In Bitcoin, proof of work requires miners to search nonces for a header hash meeting a target; the accepted valid chain has the greatest cumulative work. More confirmations make rewriting history harder under the network’s security assumptions. Benefits include shared auditability and tamper evidence. Costs include proof-of-work energy use, throughput/latency limits, public-data privacy issues, key loss, and difficult correction of erroneous entries. Blockchain is not an absolute guarantee of truth or immutability, and not all blockchains use proof of work.
discussions.teach: Hashes connect history; signatures authorize spending; consensus resolves competing histories. None does all three jobs alone.
discussions.example: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part.
discussions.correct: Hash links plus validation and consensus create a shared tamper-evident history
distractors: Encryption alone makes every transaction private
A nonce is the owner’s password
Every blockchain must use Bitcoin mining

discussions.title: Bitcoin and ownership transfer
discussions.answer: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer digital currency whose transaction history is recorded on a blockchain. A spender authorizes use of earlier unspent transaction outputs by satisfying their spending conditions, typically with a digital signature created using the spender’s private key. A new output specifies conditions for the receiver. Nodes verify authorization and check for double spending; mining orders valid transactions through proof of work. SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest) contributes to hashing and proof of work, not encryption of a coin. An address is commonly derived from a key or script and is not always the raw public key. Public ledger transparency provides pseudonymity, not guaranteed anonymity. Miners receive a block subsidy and transaction fees as incentives.
discussions.teach: Ownership means the ability to authorize spending under the output’s rules. You transfer spending rights through a transaction; you do not email a secret coin file.
discussions.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.
discussions.correct: A peer-to-peer currency with signature-authorized spending and blockchain consensus
distractors: A coin encrypted with SHA-256 and emailed
A central-bank database with no signatures
An anonymous password shared by all miners

discussions.title: Metasploit and SET business case
discussions.q: A staff member used a fake login page, then the workstation made an unusual outbound connection. Explain the possible business impact, useful evidence, and layered response.
discussions.answer: The fake login may have disclosed credentials, putting accounts and accessible business records at risk. The unusual connection warrants investigation but does not alone prove a reverse shell or data theft. Correlate the login timeline, endpoint processes and files, destination details, and available proxy, flow, and packet evidence. Follow the incident plan to contain affected systems and preserve evidence; reset compromised credentials from a trusted device, revoke sessions, and investigate related account activity. Endpoint execution may require host recovery in addition to account remediation. Prevent recurrence with independent verification, filtering, phishing-resistant authentication, least privilege, patching, application controls, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), and appropriate egress policy. Explain the distinct limits: patches do not stop every fake login, TLS (Transport Layer Security) does not fix an already compromised endpoint, and an outbound connection is not automatically trusted.
discussions.teach: Explain the weakness, business consequence, evidence, and defense. Exact tool-menu commands are not the stated exam priority.
discussions.example: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions.
discussions.correct: Structured testing and social-engineering simulation reveal technical and human weaknesses
distractors: SET is a hash algorithm
Patching alone prevents every fake-login attack
A captured password always means code executed on the host

setting.object: An analyst needs evidence about traffic leaving a company laptop.

setting.example: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events.

foundations.q: What is DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service)?
foundations.answer: Distributed Denial of Service. An availability attack using multiple sources to overwhelm or exhaust a target’s resources.
foundations.teach: Distributed Denial of Service. An availability attack using multiple sources to overwhelm or exhaust a target’s resources.
foundations.example: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern.
foundations.correct: Distributed Denial of Service. An availability attack using multiple sources to overwhelm or exhaust a target’s resources.
distractors: Cross Site Scripting. Injection that causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a victim browser in a trusted site’s context.
SQL Injection. Untrusted input changes the structure or meaning of a database query. Parameterized queries separate commands and data.
Malicious code attached to a host file or document that replicates when the host runs.

setting.object: Customers cannot use a website because an attacker occupies its connection-handling capacity.
setting.location: The web server and the network or application connections it handles.
setting.purpose: Keep the service usable for legitimate customers.
setting.action: SYN floods target connection setup; Slowloris holds web requests incomplete. Match mitigation to the exhausted resource rather than assuming every attack needs enormous bandwidth.
setting.example: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern.

setting.object: A website accepts user input, queries a database, and displays results in a browser.

foundations.answer: Rivest Shamir Adleman. An asymmetric cryptographic family named for Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman. Classroom arithmetic uses products of primes and modular exponents.

setting.object: A classroom program encrypts and decrypts a small integer using a toy RSA (Rivest Shamir Adleman) example.
setting.location: The program’s selected primes, modulus, exponents, and modular calculations.
setting.purpose: Understand the mathematical relationship between public and private exponents.
setting.action: Choose e coprime to φ(n), and d so ed leaves remainder one modulo φ(n). The small unpadded example teaches arithmetic and is not suitable for real confidential data.
setting.example: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7.

32.action: A keylogger records keystrokes. Transport encryption does not protect input already observed on a compromised endpoint; physical and software controls address different variants.

33.purpose: Reduce unnecessary exposure and enforce appropriate access and execution rules.
33.action: Use standard accounts, patch software, disable unneeded services, configure host protections, and verify required settings. NAC (Network Access Control), GPO (Group Policy Object), endpoint firewalls, and HIPS (Host Intrusion Prevention System) perform different jobs.

38.purpose: Keep the contents readable by the intended recipient and independently verify signed content.
38.action: Public-key encryption for Bob uses Bob’s public key and corresponding private decryption key. Alice signs with her private signing key; verification uses her trusted public key. Hybrid systems combine public-key techniques with symmetric data protection.

44.object: A traveler sees a wireless network name that looks like the hotel’s network.
44.location: The Wi-Fi selection screen, access point, and any captive login page.
44.purpose: Avoid treating a copied name or convincing page as proof of a trusted operator.
44.action: Displayed names and identifiers can be spoofed. Verify the intended network and service rather than relying on the familiar label alone.

54.purpose: Distinguish processing rules and security requirements instead of treating every construction as the same.
54.action: Substitution replaces symbols; XOR combines bits; block and stream ciphers process data differently. Secure randomness, correct key use, confusion, and diffusion have distinct roles; a true one-time pad is never reused.

62.location: The implemented protocol, algorithm, software, and device resources.
62.purpose: Provide appropriate security without ignoring implementation errors or operating limits.
62.action: Weak algorithms, forced weaker settings, and programming mistakes create different problems. Resource limits affect implementation choices but do not justify assuming insecure choices are safe.

65.location: Control equipment, associated computers, and the monitoring information they provide.
65.purpose: Recognize that compromised components can produce misleading observations.
65.action: The Stuxnet example connects targeted compromise with deceptive monitoring. Independent evidence and appropriate system boundaries matter.

66.object: A company wants to deny an address, block website categories, and prevent unapproved programs from running.
66.location: Network rules, application intermediaries, and endpoint execution policy.
66.purpose: Choose enforcement at the place where the unwanted action happens.
66.action: Firewall or ACL (Access Control List) rules can block traffic attributes; proxies can enforce application policies; application allowlisting restricts execution. Merely observing an event is not the same as preventing it.

70.location: An employee’s screen and the source of the warning.
70.purpose: Verify the claim without following an attacker’s instructions.
70.action: Use known trusted security tools and support channels. A professional appearance and urgent wording do not establish that a warning is legitimate.

79.object: An administrator selects services for web access, file transfer, email, device management, and clock synchronization.
79.location: Clients, servers, protocol configuration, and communication paths.
79.purpose: Choose the correct service and verify what protection is actually provided.
79.action: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), FTPS (File Transfer Protocol over Transport Layer Security), SFTP (Secure Shell File Transfer Protocol), S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), and SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) protect different applications. DNS (Domain Name System), SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), and NTP (Network Time Protocol) have distinct jobs; their ordinary names do not guarantee every security property.

84.location: The provider’s infrastructure and the customer’s applications, accounts, data, and configuration.

84.action: SaaS (Software as a Service) supplies an application; PaaS (Platform as a Service) supplies a platform; IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) supplies infrastructure. Responsibilities depend on the service arrangement and do not disappear when moving to the cloud.

When two concurrent threads of execution access a shared resource simultaneously, resulting in unintended consequences
